div.head: McDOUGALL'S Paterit SELF-RAISING FLOUR Btl!Ep.B2:rinr.
div.p: McDOUGALL'S Paterit SELF-RAISING FLOUR Btl!Ep.B2:rinr.
FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

Summer so long delayed seems to have come all at once with a rush, and from wearing heavy serge and cloth gowns we were at very short notice obliged to don airy muslins and cool linens. The wise woman who has foreseen some such con- tingency will reap the benefit of her fore- sight in the dainty toilettes already pro- vided and ready for immediate wear, while her less thoughtful sisters are beseiging the overworked dressmakers and modistes with vain petitions for summer gowns, and are obliged to wait patiently the time that these autocrats of the realms of dress find it con- venient to gratify their desires and send home the sorely-needed dresses and hats. The short or trotteur skirt is in great demand for seaside and country wear, and the plissé soled skirt is one of the favourite modes, as it gives ample concession to a graceful outline such as fashion and good taste demand. The best materials for this style of skirt consist either of a fine serge or a Shantung silk, as they are not easily crushed, and keep well in pleats. A cream serge skirt plissé and a short-pleated bolero trimmed with filet lace, together with a
A SMART MODE.

wide silk band, make a charming boating toilette; while the bright, rich blue .which closely resembles royal blue, and is so popular a colour in Paris for smart gowns, has much to recommend it to the votaries of La Mode on this side of the Channel. The smart and modish toilette sketched is of light blue serge trimmed with coarse lace in a novel and chic style. The skirt boasts an empiecement of lace from which the pleats spring. It is worn with a toque of folded tulle softened by lace and enhanced by a curling ostrich feather. This gown would also look well carried out in fine cream serge or tussore silk.

filouses are still as warmly welcomed as ever, being a grateful change from the tight boned dress bodice, which made life a burden almost too grievous to be borne on a hot summer's afternoon. There are some de- lightful embroidered linen blouses for morn- ing wear, which do not crush or soil so easily as those of silk or muslin; while the pretty flowered delaines or the fine twill flannels with Paisley-patterned borders are as charm- ing as they are popular. There are alsc elaborate afternoon blouses made of silk,

lace, and embroidery intermingled togethet with many cunning little tucks, and very charming and cool are those made of fine spotted or plain muslin interspersed with insertion and tucks. Some particularly pretty and simple blouses I recently admired were of 4fine whit o spotted muslin, made in cross-over style, showing a V at the throat, the edge of which and round the neck and down the front being finished by a band of coloured embroidery. These were quite out

of the common, and so simple as to be easily made by anyone with clever fingers. The pretty tea-gown depicted is of soft muslin trimmed with made frills of lace- edged muslin. The shoulders have a soft fichu of muslin draped round them, which ,is caught together at the front by a gold buckle, and falls from there in long ends down the front of the skirt. This style of tea-gown is easily slipped on and delightfully cool on a hot summer's day, but it could be made of a thicker material if desired, such as delaine or fine flannel, with the fichu of spotted muslin, cor white washing silk. Those of -.us who haws

div.head: AN EVENING BLOUSES
div.p: AN EVENING BLOUSES

yielded to the charm of these delightfully comfortable gowns find them irresistible, and cannot exist without something of the sort close at hand, to be slipped on when one comes in wet and tired, or heated and ex- hausted, as the case may be. The evening blouse sketched is for dinner wear, being made of cream silk with deep frills of accordion-pleated chiffon to matchd The front of the decolletage is shaped in a very becoming manner, and is finished by a band of pearl embroidery. One of the newest styles of bodices shows a deep rounded piece, shaped like a bib, which conceals the front of the bodice almost to the waist, edged by a quilling of lace or ribbon, or by some knotted silk fringe. The skirt worn with a bodice of this style has a rounded apron-like piece, which is rounded off at the back, where it is finished by a bow and long ends of silk. The edge of the over-skirt is trimmed to match the bib on the bodice. This is practically. a revival of the tunique of a quarter of a century ago. There is something very quaint about this mode, but it is hardly likely as yet to be generally worn. _

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The King himself has twice been brought back from the gates of death by skilful doctoring and assiduous nursing, and his Majesty and also Queen Alexandra, have always shewn the greatest personal interest in the care and cure of the sick. it has .been the constant endeavour of the King to increase the funds of the London hospitals, and his Majesty manifested his con- tinued interest in these institutions by recently attend- I ing Divine service at St. Paul's Cathedral, and paying a visit to the London Hospital, which relieves more I patients than probably any other institution in the world. It was here that the Finsen light cure for lupus ' was first introduced in the London hospitals. Professor Finsen had previously established the treatment in Den- mark, to which country he belonged, and it was entirely at the Queen's suggestion that it was brought into use at the London hospitals. The King and Queen's attendance at St. Paul's Cathedral was a week in advance of Hospital Sunday, but their Majesties were unable to be present On the appointed day, and accordingly the offertories at St. Paul's were taken a week earlier than was the case at other churches. It is only on two or three occasions in the course of the year, that an offertory is made at the Sunday services in St. Paul's Cathedral. The Dean and Chapter have been urged many times to make a collection every Sunday, it being pointed out to them by well meaning friends how much could be done with the money, but they have always replied that in their opinion it is well that there should be at least one church in London where people are at liberty to worship without being asked to give money. The number of Society weddings that have taken place this month is quite remarkable. Lady Juliet Lowther made a very handsome, stately bride, in her exquisite robe of point d'Alencon lace over white satin, and Lady Mary Grosvenor, also in white satin veiled with priceless lace looked very girlish, and particularly graceful. Both these brides have received many joint wedding gifts, an idea which happily is be- coming very popular. How many less distinguished brides who have received innumerable butter dishes, cruets, fish-carvers, etc., would have been thankful to have had in theirplaces, a few really useful, handsome gifts ? The Duke and Duchess of Teck,Lord and Lady Ormonde' Lord and Lady Shaftesbury, and other mem- bers of Lady Mary Grosvenor's family, presented her with a set of diamond stars convertible into a tiara' or bodice ornaments, while Georgina Lady Dudley, Lord and Lady Wolverton, Lord and Lady Farquhar and several of Lord Dudley's brothers, presented Lady Mary —nowLady.Crichton—with an oak chest of silver. One of Lord Cnchton's presents was an old brass door knocker, in the form of a grotesque figure, and modelled perfectly. This was a decided original gift, and was much admired. The Grand Duke and Duchess of Mecklenbury, Strelitz, are this month celebrating their diamond wedding. With the exception of her brother the Duke of Cambridge, the Grand Duchess is the oldest member of our Royal Family, and she was married in 1843. The Duke of Cambridge who has lived a strenuous life, and has never spared himself in his public duties, is no longer able to bear his advanced age with his former vigour, but the Grand Duchess is still hale and not only pays occasional visits to London, but takes the keenest interest in the doings of Society. King Victor Emmanuel, who has put off his visit until the autumn, has been little in this country, but he is sure of a very hearty welcome when he arrives as the • guest of his Majesty. King Victor is thirty-three years of age, and since his accession to the throne three veps ago he has become much more popular with the Italian people. He is neither so tall nor fine looking as his father, but he has lost the weakness that threatened him with consumption in his youth, and the haughtiness that characterized him has quite disappeared. His pet hobby is the collecting of coins and medals, and he is even more devoted to numismatics than our Prince of Wales is to his famous collection of stamps. Lady Henry Somerset, who recently retired from the presidency of the British Women's TemperanceAssocia- Lion, which she hasheld since 1890, was quite a society leader at one time. The eldest daughter of Earl and Countess Somers, she did not change her name to any noticeable extent when she married in 1873 Lord Henry Somerset, the second son of the then Duke of Beaufort. Whilst, however, occuping a leading position in the world of rank and fashion, Lady Henry suddenly gave up fashionable life, and devoted her time to good works amongst the poor. It was this that made her such a staunch adherent to the temperance movement, as she quickly found that drink was principally the cause of poverty and misery amongst the poor. The Dore gallery, famous for its pictures, has this week been the scene of an exhibition organised by the Dress Designers' Society, which was formed a few months ago, to encourage art in feminine attire. One looks at such an exhibition from the picturesque rather than from the practical point of view, and though some of the specimen costumes were attractive, they were mostly priced too high to be of more'than passing interest to people with moderate means. The Society may, however, do useful work by encouraging com- petition, and some of the exhibits sent by different Schools of Art, and especially. those of hand woven dress materials, lace, embroideries, millinery, 3:c., were very beautiful as specimens of work. The Queen has lately made several purchases of Irish poplins to be worn by her Majesty on the occasion of the Royal visit to Ireland. These materials are quite old favourites with the Queen and Royal Princesses and it was only to be expected that her Majesty would show her preference for them whilst on a visit to the Irish people. With this object in view the Queen has made a large selection of plain, corded, figured, and brocaded poplins, in many cases with shamrock designs, and toilettes of these beautiful materials will not only be worn by her Majesty but also by all the ladies of the Court. .

Elbow sleeves for outdoorgala toilettes are having a great vogue this su-nmer. Last year they were much in evidence at fashionable American watering places, and on the French seaboard they are always to be seen invariably finished with deep ruffles of lace, and a turned back brocade gauntlet. Many women to whom the matter of long gloves is a serious item, have little elbow to wrist sleeves built with such gowns, which can easily be tacked in for less dressy occasions. The craze for tassels is now numbered among the past so far as the modish woman is concerned. The cheaper costume is profusely adorned in this manner, and lead- ing modistes have quite finished with the idea. The same state of affairs must shortly obtain concerning the fichu of marabout and ostrich feathers ,which falls in long ends, almost to the feet, in front. This is to be regretted as few coverings or wraps have proved so generally becoming. But they unfortunately lend them- selves well to cheap imitation, and consequently their career in the world of fashion is almost at an end. MADGE.

div.head: DOCTOR SAID INCURABLE! REFUSED £2O! Yet Bile Beans Restored her to Health. LIVER TROUBLE AND INDIGESTION CURED!
div.p: DOCTOR SAID INCURABLE! REFUSED £2O! Yet Bile Beans Restored her to Health. LIVER TROUBLE AND INDIGESTION CURED!

If ever you hear it said that chronic liver disorder, indigestion, and allied ailments are "incurable," just bear in mind the following copy of a legal document duly signed and attested before a Commissioner:— "I, Jane Coxon, of 55, Kensington-road, Southport, in the County of Lancashire, do solemnly and sincerely declare as follows :—I have suffered for over forty years from acute headache, biliousness, indigestion, and weakness brought on by these ailments. My liver was out of order, and in recent years I suffered from gall stones, which I passed on three occasions. For days together I ha ie been almost unable to holdup myhead. I At one time my indigestion was so severe that every- I thing I took had to come up again, and I was told the I coating had come off my stomach. S-- tir- when suffering from biliousnesr '--id
some times . --g s, I shout. have shivering fits which would come on at intervals of a few minutes.

"To one doctor :I offered twenty pounds if be could cure me, andhe assured me that neither he nor anyone elsecould do that. It was an impossibility. I believe that had it not been for Charles Forde's bile beans I should have died.

This medicine was brought to my notice by a woman living at Fenton, in Staffordshire, where my daughter lives. Bile Beans cured that woman when all other remedies had failed, and on her recommendation I de- cided to try them. I gave them a fair trial ;persevered with their use ; acted in accordance with the directions given with them; and the result is, they have now cured me. So great and beneficial has been their effect upon me, that whereas for forty years I was obliged to have some one to do my household work for me, now at the advanced age of 67, I am sufficiently strong and healthy to dispense with a servant and to do all my own work. lam only too pleased to tell any sufferers what I have found out about the wonderful power of this great vegetable medicine. And I make this solemn declaration, conscientiously believing the same to be true, and by virtue of the Statutory Declaration Act, 1835. "(Signed) JANE COXONI. Declared by the said Jane Coxon, at Southport, in the County of Lancashire, this Bth day of May, 1903, before me. _

"(Signed) R. ASHTON FLETCHER." Chas. Forde's bile beans succeed where all other medi- cines fail, and they are obtainable from all medicine vendors at Is. fld. or 2s. 9d. per box. Don't take sub- stitutes.

The British Conference of the Young Men's Christian Association was opened in Bristol on Tuesday and will be continued throughout the week. A large number of delegates attended, including representatives from the colonies. On the recommendation of the Finance Com- mittee it was decided to mise a fund of one million shillings for the extension of the work of the Association. On Thesday afternoon Messrs. Sotheby sold by auction a Victoria Cross, which was awarded to Ser- geant Henry Ramage, of the 2nd Dragoons, for rescuing a comrade in the charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava. Ramage did not survive many months after receiving his cross. Bidding started at £25, and was carried by successive changes to £6l, it being purchased by Messrs. Spink.

div.head: Examiner Friday, June 19, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner Friday, June 19, 1903.

THE
BY HARRIS BURLAND, AUTHOR OF bACOBR4,ETC.
CHAPTER 111
"THE BODY OF THIS DEATH."

THE two men looked at each other ant Treclegar nodded his head in answer to th: mute enquiry in Hughes' eyes. Then the) too;: up the, limp bodies one by one in then arm; and carried them into the thickest par of the forest. When thcy reached the under. growth they scraped four shallow graves ir the soft rotting mould, and stamping dowr the earth, covered, the places with tanglec masses of orchid and palm. Then they re: turned with a grim look in their faces. There was only one thought in their minds, only one hope—that they might find the creature and avenge the dead.' All fear had vanished. They fet, nothing of the silence, and the lonelines.3, and the unknown terror crouching in the lepths of the forest, and waiting for their li7es. They only saw that something had to be killed, and they were resolved to kill it.

They made a complete circuit of the open part of tie forest, looking everywhere, and listening intently for any sound, but they did not hear 1r see anything of what they sought. They made up their minds to spend the night in the place. They had with them some fish that they had dried in the sun and a bottle of water. They made a meal off this frugal fare, and searched for a suitable place to keep their watch through the darkness.

They selected the most open spot they could find, and piled up a huge heap of brush- wood. There they stayed till the sun set, and as the darkness came swiftly over the heavens they once more began to realise the supernatural fear of the forest, a fear of things unseen and unknown, a lurking terror that watched them from the shadows. This was no physical fear, though they knew that the thing they sought would have them at a dis- advantage, and that darkness would be all in its favour. They were both brave men, and one of them endowed with enormous bodily strength. They feared nothing that they could grasp and battle with. But they began to see how, after all that had happened, the very darkness itself would be their enemy. Yet they knew that the creature would only attack in the darkness, and it was their one chance to kill it.

They lit their fire, and sitting back to back strained every nerve to see and hear. The flames cast a wide circle of red light, giving a weird effect to the gnarled and stunted trees. In the gloom beyond Tredegar thought he could see the faces of his dead comrades. He placed his rifle across his knees, and kept watch with his hands on the barrel. It would at least be something to strike with, and Tredegar meant to strike hard. Hughes grasped his bludgeon tightly, and stared into the crackling flames.

After three hours of this silent watch, Tredegar's eyes grew drowsy with sleep, and it required a great mental effort to keep them oDen. He began to realise the sufferings of the sentry who knows it is death to him to sleep. From time to time the two men spoke to each other. It was necessary to keep themselves awake, and the sound of a human voice was cheerful in the great solitude. There was not a whisper in the depths of the forest, neither rustling of leaf, nor cry of bird. It was terrible to listen to such silence.

Then Tredegar noticed that Hughes' back began to press more heavily against his own, and fearing that the latter was asleep, he turned round to shake him. As he did so he heard a faint scratching such as the claws of an animal would make on a rock. He rose sharply to his feet and Hughes fell backwards. Twenty yards away something moved behind the shadow of a tree. Hughes jumped up with the startled eyes of one suddenly wakened from sleep, and stared wildly into the dark- ness. The fire was low and Tredegar flung a pile of brushwood on the red embers. But he flung too much of it, and the dense smoke smothered the struggling flames, and only a shower of sparks illuminated the darkness. Then one branch commenced to burn furiously and Hughes sprang forward with an oath.

A second later there was a terrific thud, and Tredegar heard the crack of wood, and saw Hughes' bludgeon fly into the air in two pieces He rushed forward, and as he did so Hughes was flung backwards with so terrific a force that he twice turned head over heels on the ground. Tredegar saw something move before him, and swinging the rifle over his shoulder, he struck at it with all his gigantic strength. The barrel snapped and the stock went spinning into the forest, striking half a dozen trees before it fell to the ground. He rushed back to the fire and kicked the smouldering brushwood till it burst into a clear flame. Then he went back to look at the thing he had struck. He expected to find it dead or maimed, for few living things could have stood up against such a blow. But he only found a livid scar across the dark trunk of a tree, and a dent two inches deep in the wood, and fragments of bark on the ground. But in the distance he still heard something move.

He turned to Hughes who was lying motion- less on his back. He lifted the limp form off the ground into a sitting position and looked into the face. It was white and drawn, and the blood trickled down one side of it from a gash in the forehead. Tredegar thrust his hand against the heart, but could discern no movement. Then he placed the blue steel barrel of the rifle against the lips and the surface did not dull. He examined the body closely and turned it over. The man's back was broken, and he was quite dead. Tredegar was alone on the island with a monster that had killed four men and a boy as easily as a child kills flies. He rose to his feet and stared .at the dark ring of forest around him, while the whole horrible truth burst upon his brain. He was alone in the island. He muttered the word " alone " to himself, and tried to realise all it meant. All the silence; the solitude, the long, empty days, the sleepless nights, the years, crawling by one after another till his hair grew grey and his body was bent with age. The loss of all interest in life, the loss, pehaps, of reason, itself, or the power of human speech, till he became a mere animal, dragging out its bestial existence in the forest. All this he saw before him in the darkness. The fairest island in the world could hold all the torments of hell for a lonely man. But this loathsome spot, tenanted by foul spiders and by something else that would be a constant tetror till it had been destroyed, had such inconceivable horrors of its own that the mind could not grasp them. And then Mavanwy—, Tre- degar could think no more. He fell on his knees and prayed that he might not think— prayed that he might die, that he might go mad, that he might do anything but think and realise his position. Then he cried out to Heaven aloud, so that he might hear his own voice. The cry was answered by a savage howl in the distance. In a moment Tredegar's mood changed, and the cloud of darkness lifted from his brain. He rose to his feet and gripped the barrel of the broken rifle in his hand. Here, at any rate, was something to be done—something to take his thoughts from his loneliness— something that needed strength and nerve and skill. Here was a tangible adversary to be hunted down, to be battled with, to be lured on to an attack, to be killed. The gigantic young Welshman had no fear of the result. He would let the creature track him down, and try to kill him as it had killed his com- rades. It would find out its mistake too late. Every muscle of his body grew taut as a rope of steel. His face glowed in the firelight with the pride .)4. stsength. He grasped the -branch of a tree near to him with one hand, and, tear ing it from its socket, flung it on the fire with
a laugh. He pictured himself tearing this un- known acivrsary limb from limb. He won- dered why it did not come: It was not afraid of human Ungs, and did not know the wel- come that awaited it. •

He threw some more brushwood on the fire and kept a lonely vigil by the dead till the dawn flushed golden throughl the trees. Then he raised the body in his arms and carried it to the same place where they had buried the others the day before. He scraped out another shallow grave in the soft earth, and laid the dead man beside his comrades. Then he filled in the narrow trench and rose to his feet. His face was pale and hard, and some- thing wet glistened on his cheekbone. This man had been nothing to him, merely a rough sailor whom chance had thrown across his path. Yet somehow his death had been different to the others. He had perhaps buried the last human being he would ever see.

He covered the grave with flowers, and made his way back to their little encamp- ment. Everything was in its place, just as it had been left the day before. He flung his tired body on the sand and longed for sleep Yet it was impossible till he had made a safe place to sleep in. He roused himself to his task, and after he had eaten • some fish, he went to the edge of the forest and began to break off boughs varying from four to six inches in thickness. He carried these to the shelter and spread them over the top of the canvas. Then he took large stones from the beach and placed them on the top of the boughs. The smallest of these stones weighed at least a hundred pounds, and the whole formed a solid roof of masonry. Then he filled up the cracks between the three great boulders with wood, jammed in tightly, and strengthened on the outside by great heaps of stones. Then he turned his attention to the open side of the structure, and it was some time before he could think of a satis- factory door—something that would keep anything out, and be opened and shut from within. At last, however, he managed to drag a huge flat slab of rock against the open- ing. It left a gap of about eighteen inthes at the top, and it was just possible for him to squeeze through this. Te fill up this gap he placed a heavy log of driftwood, so balanced that it could be easily dislodged. It could only be removed from the outside by pushing it into the interior, and the noise of its fall would be sufficient to wake the soundest sleeper. _ . .

When he had finished this work to his satis- faction, he lay down on the sandy floor and went to sleep. He was worn out, and did not wake till it was dark. He struck a match and looked at his watch. It had stopped. He had forgotten to wind it during the ex- citement of the last thirty-six hours. He rose to his feet, and, removing the wooden barrier, looked out into the darkness. It was a starlight night, but he could see nothing except a dark mass of forest against thesky and the reflection of a few stars in the water. It was the first night there had been no genial glow of firelight, and he realised how much this means to a lonely man. He wound up his watch, and the mere clicking of the wheels was a grateful sound. He lit a match, and held it outside the opening. In the little circle of light he could see the grey spiders moving to and fro. He shuddered. Then he foraged for some dried fish, took a deep draught of water, and leant back against one of the boulders which formed the walls of his little fortress. In spite of the darkness he was wide awake. He would have been glad to have been able t 0 sleep till daybreak, but he found it impossible to close his eyes. They were fixed on a narrow gap of sky,that faced him, and he counted the stars that twinkled through the opening till they seemed like little flames dancing across the darkness. Suddenly half of the stars vanished as though a cloud of smoke had been driven across them, and something darker than the sky „moved in the opening. At the same time Tredegar heard the heavy breathing of some animal and the scraping of something against the slab of stone. lie laughed quietly to himself from the darkness of his corner, and leaning noiselessly forward, gripped the log of wood and drew it slowly towards him across the sand. As he did so the form dis- appeared, the great slab of stone swung back- wards, and then fell forward against the boulders with a crash. Tredegar laughed to himself. He had dragged that slab of stone forty yards, -and this creature could barely shift it from its place. Then once more there was a dark, shadowy outline against the sky. Tredegar lifted the log of wood and poised it in the air. A second later it went spinning forward to the opening like a missile hurled form some ancient man- gonel. But it turned over, in its flight, and one end striking the roof, it crashed against the stone slab with such force that the whole structure trembled. There was a howl of rage or pain from the darkness, a blind scuffle, and the crashing of the stone slab as it swung backwards and forwards in quick succession. Tredegar gripped the barrel of the rifle, which he had kept by his side, and waited. Then he struck a match with -.his left hand, and looked at the gap. There, peering above the stone was a horrible mass of yellow aid matted hair, out of which glittered a pair of malignant eyes. And stretched over the top a great hairy limb and long claws which grasped and scraped the stone, as though they would tear it to pieces. Then the match burned down to his fingers and they were in darkness. He sprang for- ward with a cry and clutched the limb. It was hard as steel and wrenched itself from his clasp, leaving a tuft of hair in his hand. Then he bore all his strength and weight against the slab of stone and hurled it to the ground. It fell with a heavy thud on the sand, and Tredegar moved cautiously out of the shelter looking sharply right and left in case of a surprise. But nothing attacked him, and for a moment or two he could hear nothing but the tumultuous beating of his own heart. Then listening intently he heard soft foot- falls in the distance, and shortly afterwards the snapping of twigs and rustling of branches in the forest. The creature had fled from him. Perhaps it had thought better of its intentions after it had felt the grip of Trede- gar's hand. At any rate it had fled, and Treclegar bit his lip with vexation. He did not fear the contest. What he did fear was the continual terror of watching and waiting for his adversary, the sense of death lurking behind every tree and stone, and concealing itself in every shadow. He resolved to put the matter to an issue there and then. He guessed that this creature feared the light, and like other beasts of pre', preferred to prowl in the night time. All his comrades, except the boy, had been seized after hark, and it was probable that the boy had run right into the creature's hiding place. It was no use, therefore, to wait for the dayligat The thing probably had some secret lair, which he might never find. It was necessary to tempt it to an attack, and this would have to be done by night. He picked the rifle barrel from the floor and made his way across the sand to the forest.

He noticed in the faint light that there was not 4. spider to be seen on the shore. Doubt- less they had been disturbed and had fled back into the trees. He was glad that they and gone. It would nit have been pleasant to walk over a thick carpet of their bodies. When he reached the trees he found the pathway which they had already cut throtigh the forest and groped 'blindly along it in the darkness. So long as he kept to the path he moved ahead slowly and with steps that often stumbled as they caught some rut or stone, but directly he was confronted by =Ss Of thorny bushes. .or a net-work of

creepers, or a trunk of a tree, he knew that he had left the track. It was laborious work. The gloom was intense, almost overwhelming in its oppressive blackness. The air was hot and scented with innumerable flowei.:, and spices. Tredegar felt that he was bu under some gigantic pall, drenched with the perfumes of Araby. Every now and then he stopped and listened, expecting to heat the snapping of a twig or the soft crunching oi feet in the thick mould. He heard nothing but a long continuous rustle, so faint as to be almost imperceptible. He knew that it was the movement of millions of spiders. His face brushed against their webs. He could feel their tiny legs on his hands, and .his clothes were covered with them. It was a loathsome journey, but there was that in his mind which forbade him to turn- back. He only prayed that. he might find what he sought as soon as possible. He kept every nerve and muscle on the alert, ready at any moment to strike or free himself from the grasp of an adversary. _ _

But it was not Until he had reached the more open part of the forest that his prayer was answered. He had just emerged close to the place where the bodies of his comrades were buried when the end of the rifle barrel was seized and wrenched so violently that Treclegar would have fallen if he had not been prepared for su- han emergency. He could see nothing, but shifting his hands farther down the barrel to get a greater leverage he encountered a huge hairy paw and felt the cold touch of metal against his fingers. At the same time something jingled against the rifle barrel as they swayed to and fro in the darkness.

Tredegar hesitated whether to let go and seize his . adversary by the throat, but he thought the risk too great. A steel rifle barrel is a nasty weapon and he could not afford to lose it on the chance of getting a good and certain grip. He tugged and strained with all his strength, and flung his adversary to and fro in his efforts to shake him off. But the creature held on, and in its turn tried to throw Treclegar off his feet. At last they both stood still, and tried by slow pressure to force the barrel out of each other's hands.

Then slowly, inch by inch, the rifle began to bend under the enormous strain till it was curved like a bow. Then suddenly it snapped and both reeled backwards. The next second Tredegar was flung to the ground with a great pair of hairy claws at his throat. He had not been quick enough. Powerful though he was, it was evident that this crea- ture had the advantage of him in activity. Man is one of the least active of all animals. It was possible, too, that the thing could see in the dark, and had him at a disadvantage. Tredegar gripped the limbs and by sheer strength bent them backwards till the fingers grew loose at his throat and the animal shrieked with Pain. Then he swung the thing downwards to the ground, and still holding the limbs, tried to struggle to his feet. But the task was too much for him. When he had struggled to his knees the creature managed to twist itself round with such force that it wrenched itself from his grasp. He rose in a flash to his feet, but before he could get another hold it went crashing through the forest in flight. But it had left something in Tredegar's hand —something semi-circular and hard and cold like half of a metal disc. Tredegar thrust it into his pocket and started off, in pursuit. He was determined to finish the contest that ni •-ht. His blood was up and he knew he could do himself justice. He was only afraid that the creature would seek to avoid him now that it knew what sort of a man it had to deal with.

The chase was hopeless from the first. Tredegar, even if he had been as active as his opponent, could scarcely have followed him in the dark at an equal pace. He was only guided by sound, and from time to time he had to stop and listen. Every minute the swish of boughs and rustle of leaves grew fainter and fainter in the distance. He was bruised from head to foot and bleeding from a hundred scratches. Every now and then he came crashing down on to his hands as his foot caught in some rut or creeper. At last the trees began to thin and diminish in size, and the stars began to shine through their branches, and he heard the distant sound of the sea. In five minutes' time he staggered out on to the edge of the cliffs and felt the cold night air blowing from the ocean._ ...

-Beneath himC the heavy Pacific surge thundered on the rocks and even where he stood, some sixty feet above it, the salt spray beat against his face. Far away on the horizon a thin bar of grey showed the coming of the dawn.

He sat down a few yards from the edge and rested his face in his hands. All the lust of blood and the heat of contest had died away. He only saw the great loneliness. The very voice of the sea seemed to whisper the word " Alone." The faint rustle of the breeze in the stunted trees behind him seemed to echo it. He was alone—alone! And once more through the darkness he saw the slate cliffs of Cardiganshire, and the foam running up their sides, and the little village straggling by the sea, and the ring of . purple mountains towering peak after peak into the distance. And once more he saw the face of Mavanwy —white, tired with waiting, yet patient with love. And once more he heard her voice, and she whispered the word "Alone." He clenched his hands in agony. He could not endure these thoughts, and for one moment the brink of the cliff seemed dangerously near to him. It was but a step •or two, and then-- No, he was no coward to shirk what lay before him ! He would wait. One year, two years, three perchance, and then— the ship, the stray vessel driven out of its course, the signal on the heights, flag or fire, the boat sweeping towards him across the sea. The sight of a human face, the touch of a human hand, the sound of a human voice. It was worth waiting for. Yet it might never come. There might be no dawn in the awful night that loomed'beiore liin As if in answer t. his thoughts, the grey bar on the horizon lightened into pale yellow, and then into a brilliant gold; and then the whole Eastern sky glowed with azure and rose, and the sea itself was a lake of rippling fire. He rose to his feet, and his rough face seemed to drink in the light, as a thirsty man drinks in water.

As the sun crept up from the sea he saw that he was on a part of the coast he had never visited before. The trees ran almost to the edge of the cliffs. He took the compass from his pocket and saw that he was almost exactly on the opposite side of the island to the little encampment. He resolved to ex- plore the coast before returning to the creek, and knowing that the shore must eventually lead him to his destination, he started to walk along the cliffs.

Before he had gone very far he chanced to thrust his hands into his pockets, and his fingers encountered the metal disc he had wrenched off in the contest of the night before. He examined it carefully, and saw that it was made of some yellow metal, per- haps gold, and had evidently been fastened to Something else by a short piece of chain, which was still attached to it. Only half of the gold disc remained. It had evidently been broken off, for the edges were jagged and uneven. At the first glance Tredegar concluded that the other half had been torn off in the struggle ; but a more careful inspec- tion of the edge showed that it was dull and worn, and that the fracture was of long stand- ing. The disc was covered with Strange let- tering, which as absolutely unintelligible tc Tredegar. It seemed, however, that he recognised some of the letters.. The whole disc must have been over three inches across, and an eighth of an inch in thickness. He turned it over and over in his hand, but could make nothing of it. But the horrible suspicion crossed his mind that the creature that sought his life and which had taken the lives of his comrades was or had been a human being. No animal, he.reasoned, would have such a thing fastened to its limbs, unless indeed ' it had been placed there by human beings. But he could surmise no more than this from the dull yellow surface.

Ile replaced it in his pocket and continued his walk along the coast. After he had gone about a mile the cliffs began to rise higher and higher from the shore beneath, till their sum- mits were three hundred feet above the sea.

Then they were suddenly split by a ravine. At first 'rredegar thought he had reached the narrow channel by which they had originally landed on the island. But when he reached the edge he saw that tins • was not the case. Far below him the sea beat with great fury on an evil-looking reef, and sluiced backwards and forwards between piles of jagged rock. Be- hind the reef lay a little pool of smooth water that rippled gently 'on a sandy beach. The whole ravine was in the form of a wedge, and its apex Was not more than three hundred yards from the water. Its sides dropped sheer down to a floor of soft white sand, piled up in long ridges and dunes and dotted here and there with clumps of straggling shrub and thin, wiry grass. Some twenty yards from the edge of the water the sand rose in a great hillock, and something dirk jutted -out from one of the sides. Tredegar's curiosity was roused. It looked remai .ably like a wreck buried in the sand. He walked along the edge of the precipice to the extreme point where a narrow bank of shale sloped down steeply to a huge heap of boulders that had been broken off from the rocky walls, and heaped up to a height of more than one hun- dred feet. A little stream trickled down the slope and poured a tiny cascade of water over the edge of a large rock.

He -descended , with considerable difficulty to the beach, and ploughed his way ankle- deep through the dry, silvery sand to the strangely-shaped hillock by the water. And as he went he saw that which quickened his pulse, and made him glance swiftly round the rocky sides of the gorge. Parallel with his own path were innumer- able deep dents in the sand. They bore no resemblance to the impression of a foot, for they were merely little funnel-shaped holes. But Tredegar looked back at his own tracks, and saw that his own feet left similar marks in the shifting yielding sand. His heart. beat high with hope. "At -last, he said to himself, -" I have tracked this horror to its lair, and it shall not leave the gorge alive ! " But he was doomed to disappointment. He was, however, right in supposing that the hillock of sand marked the grave of a vessel. As he drew near to it he saw torn beams and shattered spars sticking out from the sides, and these were white as the sand itself, bleached by the suns of centuries. For at the first glance he could see that this was no modern ship, but an old galleon: Little remained of it but the high poop and a few bare ribs of oak. The black patch he had seen from the top of the cliff had not been timber, but the entrance to a cabin. The doorway was gone, and only a dark cavity remained. _ The floor was covered deeply with sand, and Tredegar saw that this had been shifted and trodden down by something. He paused at the entrance, with clenched fists and his legs a little apart to give him a firm standing. Then he picked up a stone and flung it hard into the darkness. The stone struck wood, and rattled from wall to wall. But nothing stirred within, and there was no sound but the splashing of the waters on the shore. He drew nearer, and, lighting a match, peered cautiously into the interior. At first he could see nothing. After the brilliant sunshine outside the light of the match was no more than darkness. Then, as his eyes grew accustomed to the gloom, he saw that the cabin was empty.

He lit another match, and examined the inside. It was a room about twelve feet square, with a low ceiling. The timbers were rudely ornamented and a coat of arms with a Spanish motto was carved on one of the beams. Tredegar recognised the arms of Castille in one of the quarterings. In one corner the sand was piled • to the ceiling, and it bore the impress a body. A heavy oaken door with broken hinges lay half-buried on the floor. He lit several more matches and examined every inch of the woodwork carefully in the hope of finding some clue to the name of the vessel. But he found none. Then a sudden idea struck him. Here was the very place for him to live. A snug shelter from sun and rain; and with the door repaired and fixed, an almost impregnable fortress, where he could sleep in security. He came out into the air and glanced at the line of rocks with the foam swirling round their bases. He was thinking of the boat and how he could bring it up on the beach. To his joy he noticed a narrow channel on one side, close to the cliffs. It was no more than fifteen feet wide, and the water sluiced through it like a mill race. It was possible that there were sunken rocks beneath. But still it was an opening, and a pair of strong arms might guide a boat through it. • He returned along the cliffs to the encamp- ment, launched the boat, placed everything in it, and rowed round the coast till he reached the ravine. Only a man of his great strength would have attempted to guide an eighteen foot boat through that narrow swirling channel. And he failed in his task. The boat ran on a sunken rock and stuck there quivering like a butterfly impaled on a pin. He leapt over the side into the shallow rush- ing water, and by superhuman efforts managed to transfer everything to the shore. But his last chance of escape was gone. With no tools it would be impossible to repair the boat, even if he could save it from its present position. But in less than two hours it was broken to pieces. Then he set to work to fix up the door of the cabin, and the sun was low in the heavens before he had accomplished the job to his satisfaction. After that he commenced to clear out the sand from the interior. He had lit a fire at the entran-t behind a wall of sand, and the red light glowed through the doorway on the oaken walls. It was a laborious task, but he threw the sand out in great handfuls and scooped it away until it lay about a foot deep on the floor. He left this as a couch to sleep on. Just as he had completed the job his eye was caught by several marks on a beam which he had just uncovered. He could not distinguish them in the firelight, but they appeared to be letters. He had some smat- tering of Spanish, and striking a match, he stooped down and examined them, moving the match along from letter to letter till he had spelt out the whole sentence. Then he looked behind him in terror, as though he expected to see something. For the words were in English, and had apparently not been cut more than a few years, and they were words that struck fear into his heart and threw a terrible light on the years that lay before him.

And yet they were but a short quotation from the New Testament—" Who shall deliver to' front the body of this death ?" He rose to his feet and staggered out into the open. The sky was roofed with tossinv flame, and the land bathed in liquid gold.. There was no sound but the roar of the sea on the rocks. The black cliffs towered up around him like the walls of a dungeon. It seemed for a moment as though he were chained down in the lowest depths of hell. The living death was written over the heavens and the sea and the sky and the very silence sp, of it. He fell on his knees and prayed. "Oh Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver the body of this death." (To be continued.)

div.head: OF THE WEEK.
div.p: OF THE WEEK.
' t v4t.
SERVIAN REVOLUTION.

The greatest sensation has been. caused 'throughout Europe by the extraordinary coup etat in Servia at the end of last week. Never -since the Middle Ages, when life was held very •cheap, has there been such a political hobo- #caust, or a murderous plot so thoroughly and unreservedly carried ciut. Apart from other 'questions, for a century there has been a •deadly blood feud between the houses -of 40brenovics and Karageorgevics ; and it is ob- vious that the conspirators decided that the only way to termin ite once and for all the long series of assassinations was to wipe out completely the whole of the former dynasty, and to leave the latter without a rival. This they did with an organisation worthy of a better cause; and now the Karageorgevics stand without any royal rivals. All they have to face in the future are the superior advan- tages of a Republic and the futile claim of Prince Mirko of Montenegro. However, de- spite the horrible nature of the stilot and the wholesale murders involved, scarcely a voice has been raised throughout Europe in sym- pathy for the late King Alexander and Queen Draga, or their satellites who suffered with

them. Indeed, the whole history of King Alexander's reign has been one of misrule and unconstitutional tyranny. Himself a man of little character, he had inherited from his father a waywardness of disposition and an inherent obstinacy which made him, like many another weak man, a source of danger; especially in the hands of a strong and design- ing woman. In fact, it may justly be said that he and his consort only received what they "played up for." and what everybody realised must take place sooner or later in their turbulent country.

After a series of youthful indiscretions, King Alexander insisted, in the teeth of his people's wishes and the advice of his Ministers, in marrying a widow many years older than him- self and not of royal blood. Madame Draga lkilaschin, indeed, was of comparatively lowly extraction, and the marriage, carried out in a hole-and-corner fashion, gave the whole country the gravest offence. As Queen, Draga exem- plified the proverb of a beggar on horseback; and, in addition, she disappointed the Servians .by bearing her husband no children. The rumours and fuss at the Servian Court last year will be well remembered, when to allay the public discontent Draga gave out that a royal infant was shortly to be expected. The reaction and disappointment only doubled her -unpopularity; and a crowning touch was put to everything by her declaration that her brother, the unpopular Colonel Nicodem Lun- jevics, was to be nominated heir to the Servian -throne. Meanwhile, King Alexander despoti- cally abrogated the Constitution and made himself an absolute monarch, with the result that the whole power passed into the hands -of the hated Draga. It is, therefore, hardly

The only alternatives Pare a Republic, which Is favoured in some quarters after the centur- ies of misrule, which has shaken Servia to the very foundations. or Prince Mirko of Monte- negro, whose following is only a very small one. The coup d'etat took place on the thirty- fifth anniversary of the assassination of Michael Obrenovics. The King and Queen were quietly buried by night in the Obreno- vms vault; and the other victims were buried at the same time in the public cemetery at Belgrade. No high officials of the Church were present, and scanty service was read by two priests. Thus ended the most extraordi- nary tragedy of modern times.
THE LATE KING AND QUEEN OF SERVIA.

div.head: PRINCE PETER KARAGEORGEVITCH:
div.p: PRINCE PETER KARAGEORGEVITCH:

-surprising that out of this state of things a -serious plot arose to get rid of the Obrenovic dynasty and its bangers-on. The plot origi- nated with and was entirely carried through •by the army, the people at large being in complete ignorance of the national crisis till all was passed. When the news was announced, it was hailed with universal joy and without a single word of horror or regret, which is in itself a proof of the intense unpopularity of the King and Queen. On Thursday night last n. cordon of troops was placed round the Konak, the Servian palace, and the residences of the chief Ministers, and sixty selected officers made their way into the palace and up to the bedroom of the King and Queens Several-of the Royal guard and two or three officers, including the King's aide-de-camps, were shot down for resisting the invaders, and King Alexander and Queen Draga, who escaped to the roof, were followed and riddled with bullets.

The Prime Minister, the Minister for War, and others were also assassinated, and other Ministers were quietly arrested. Queen Draga's brothers, the Lungovics, were seized and mur- dered, while her two sisters were deported across the frontier. The whole gruesome affair was carried through in the most quiet and business-like fashion; and subsequently a manifesto was issued by the new Govern- ment, formed by M. div.head: PALMER SCHOLARSHIP.
div.p: THE PALMER SCHOLARSHIP.

The name of Mr. Ernest Palmer, a member of the celebrated biscuit firm of Huntley and Palmer, and a director of the Great Western Railway, is already well-known in the musical world by his endowment of' a scholarship at the Royal College of Music for the benefit of the natives of Berkshire. Now his name is coming before the public as the author of a much greater and further reaching scheme for the advancement of British music, which proves his desire to promote and aid our national development in this direction. With the sanction and approval of the King. who is a past president and now patron of the .Royal College of Music, Mr. Palmer, in pursuance of a scheme for this purrrise, has endowed this institution with a large sum ot money. This is to be invested and held by the College under the title of "The Royal College of Musicians Patrons Fund," and the income is to be applied for the following purposes : (i. ) the selection by expert musicians, and the -,--forin:ince at con-
ERNEST PALMER

certs given for the special prupose, either at the College or elsewhere, of orchestral and choral works of composers being British subjects; (ii.) the selection and performance of ensemble and solo music, whether vocal or instrumental, by such compbsers ; (iii.) the assistance of musical composers (being British subjects) in procuring an appearance before the public; (iv.) the provision out of surplus income, if any, of travelling scholarships for pupils of the colleges (being British subjects) of exceptional ability. The fund is to be primari.y applicable for the benefit of past or present pupils of the Royal College of Music, but full power is given to extend this benefit to any other persons, so long only as they be British subjects. This generous endowment should be of great service to British music, and all interested in the Subject will feel very grateful to Mr. Palmer in his endeavour to further this art.

div.head: – THE DIVINE SARAFI."
div.p: - THE DIVINE SARAFI."

It is now becoming an established fact, to the delight of British playgoers, that every season sees that great aitiate, "the divine Sarah," in London. So great has always been her success that she has been encouraged to turn her once occasional visits into regular annual events; and she always plays to very lull houses. This week Madame Sarahßernhardt opened at the Adelphi, and her success was as marked as ever and her recep- tion. most flat- tering in its cordiality. She has brought all
her old favour-
ites over with her and one or
two new pieces.
She opened with " Fedora " ; on
Tuesday she played " Frou- MAD,
PrOil,” and on
:ARDTa

Wednesday, " Andromaque ' and "La Tosca." The end of the week is being given- up to " Sapho," in which part Madame Sarah Bernhardt is challenging a direct comparison between herself, Miss Olga Nethersole, Madame Rejane, and *Madame Jane Hading, the latest London " Sapho." But the piece which is being awaited with the keenest interest of all is the French version of Mr, Pinero's "Iris," which Madame Bernhardt has brought over with her. It is not often that an English play is honored by being translated into French, and the event is eagerly looked forward to. Mr. Pinero in this respect is being doubly honored, as Madame Jane Hading at the Coronet produced a French version of "The Second Mrs. Tan- queray," playing the name part herself. The last-named actress is having a very interesting and successful season at the Coronet Theatre, and repeating the great impression she. made last year. Yet another French actress is also playing in London—Madame Jeanne Granier, at the Garrick, and she, too, is drawing crowded houses and making a favourable mpression on the British public. It looks as though in the future the French invasion' would rather increase fhan decrease, so great is the success of the artistes who come to London:

div.head: KHEDIVE'S VISIT.
div.p: THE KHEDIVE'S VISIT.
PRIN

sixty, and is said to be persona grata with both Austria and Russia. He has a son, Prince George, and is a brother-in-law of the Queen of Italy. He denies any complicity in or knowledge of the plot against King Alexan- der and Queen Draga, and is at the time of writing awaiting the election of the Skupst- china. Prince Peter Karageorgevics is fatriy Popular in Set-via, an stands out by himself as the obvious Kings
INONW

Yet another important foreign potentate will be seen in London this year, though his visit will be of a more or less private character. This is the Khedive, who left Egypt recently on a somewhat prolonged tour. He is, how- ever, certain to be received and entertained by His 'Majesty, as our relations with him are very close and cordial; anti many functions are sure to be organized in his honour during his stay of ten days. He is due to arrive on June 24th, and will, according to present plans, leave on July 3rd. During his visit he will occupy Sir Ernest Cassels' magnificent town house, 48, Grosvenor THE KHEDIVE OF EGYPT. Square, which

th-at financier so intimately connected with Egypt has placed at his disposal, thus he will not be a royal guest, and will be free to do as he likes. How he will be entertained by the King and Queen has not yet been announced, but it is expected that there will be a banquet at Buckingham Palace, or a week-end visit to Windsor. The Khedive is at present at Constantinople, where he spends a week. From there he proceeds to Vienna, and from there to London. After his visit to the Metropolis is concluded he intends to visit Divonne, near the Lake of Geneva, where he will spend some time before returning to Egypt for the wintar4

The Bazaar and Fete at Moore. £660 was the total amount realized by the bazaar and fete held at the Elms, Moore' in connection with All Saints' Church, Daresbury. Saturday's proceeds were the largest obtained during the three days, the respective amounts being Thursday, £2lO, Friday, £l7O, Saturday £250. div.head: MR. MADELEY'S SALARY.
div.p: MR. MADELEY'S SALARY.
ANOTHER DISCUSSION AT THE TOWN COUNCIL MEE fING. Increase Granted.

The most important recimmendation of the Museum Committee submitted to the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday evening had reference to Mr. Madeley's salary. It was recommended that the salary of Mr. Madeley, as curator and librarian be raised to £250

per annum. In moving the confirmation of the Committee's minutes, Mr. Alderman MONKS said it would, of course, be in the recollection of the members that a resolution was passed at the last meeting to reduce Mr. Madeley's salary, on the ground that the advance given him had been given in such a way as to make it ultra vires or, at any rate, out of order. The Committee thought it was due to Mr. Madeley that they should bring the question forward twain at the earliest opportunity in proper form, so that it could not be rejected merely on that ground. The impression he had of the previous discus- don was that the opposition to the payment of the full salary being continued was because of the manner in which it had be,a brought about,andhe thought it only right that the resolution should be submitted in proper form so that they should, as a matter of fairness to Mr. Madeley, say whether he was really entitled to this salary or not. The Committee felt that they would be treating Mr. Madeley shabbily indeed if he was to be put back to his old position and have his salary reduced, because he had not had an increase for something like eight years. Some two or three years ago he applied for an advance, but the Committee thought it better not to grant one, as they felt inclined to do, but told him to wait until the re-organization of the Technical Schools had been brought about. This had been done and the Committee were, as far as he knew, unanimous in making this recommendation and thus recognizing his work for the town. (Hear, hear.) In view of the services he had rendered, Mr. Madeley was fairly entitled to be paid at the rate of £250. He was an excellent public servant, he threw his whole heart into his work, and the institution over which he presided, considering the conditions, was on the whole second to no otherinstitution of a similar kind in the country. (Hear, hear.) The Museum had been classed" A 1" by the British Association in the report of their repre- sentatives who made a tour of inspection of the Museums with the idea of seeing what progress was being made in the collection and arrangement of speci- mens not merely for exhibition but for educational pur- poses. An attempt had been made within the last few years to make the Museum of some value to the children and the people of the town generally, more particularly from an educational point of view. Mr. Madeley had takena leading part in that work, a work which would help the Education Committee in the work they would have to do in the next year or two with regard to nature studies and natural history generally. He commended this proposal to the Council and hoped they would accept the recommendation of the committee. Alderman BENNETT seconded the motion. Councillor PEMBERTON said he hardly thought Alder- man Monks put the question fairly for this reason, that it seemed to be the unanimous opinion that when the matter came before the Council last time it was not fully and properly explained. Infant it was misstated. Alderman Monks claimed the £5O towards the salary of the Director of Education and the point was not argued on Mr. Madeley's abilities at all. This was the first time the Council were actually considering this question ,of Mr. Madeley's salary. The drawing of the red ' hergbig across the path seemed to be very successfully done' in this Council. Was Mr. Madeley paid for his services on the same basis as other librarians of towns of a similar size? Why should they pay more than any other towns? Was it because the rates were low or that they were well off or that their debt was so small? There were many large ratepayers in Warrington who would be pleased to get £2OO a year, and he thought Mr. Madeley could get along very well on £2OO and a house, gas, &c, free. If the Library Committee wished to spend any more money let them spend it in the interestfrof the ratepayers and have better books and better facilities for the public. There appeared to be no difficulty in tacking on £1 a week to a big official's salary, but it was a difficult thing to put a shilling on the wages of the working men who were getting under £1 a week. He moved that the minutes be passed with the exception of that relating to the advance of Mr. Madeley's salary. Councillor LORD seconded the amendment. Councillor CRAM said he was prepared to move a resolution that the salary remain at £2OO a year. Alderman BOLTON thought it was hardly fair to reduce an official's salary when he was willing to con- tinue the services he did before. He suggested that a committee be formed to report upon the advisability of establishing branch libraries, and that Mr. Madeley should be given the £5O for the extra work entailed in having charge of them. If something of that kind were done he would have no objection to the proposal. Councillor JAMES EVANS said there was a principle involved, and he had always objected to anyone holding a dual position under the Corporation. With regard to the branch circulating libraries he thought they ought not to pay prospectively. (Hear, hear.)He saw no fresh grounds for considering the salary of Mr. Madeley. He considered they had not put Mr. Madeley's salary "back," but relieved him of certain work for which he had received an extra remuneration of £5O. If they had taken the work from him surely it was sound sense to say that they were entitled to take the money away. A principle was involved, and he did not think theyshould increase salaries on the lines suggested by the Museum Committee.

Alderman BmsNErr thought, after what was said on. the matter on the previous occasion, that the recom- mendation would get through without serious criticism. They were told at first that it was a question of pro- cedure. Now it seemed to resolve itself in a matter of pure parsimony. Councillor JAMES EVANS : It is a question of pro- cedure now.

Alderman BENNETT : It is not a question of proce- dure. The question was, he continued, whether the time had not come when an official who had been with them for 30 years should or should not get an increase. The services he had rendered were of the very highest value in spite of what had been said to the contrary. He did not think there was a town in England which had a more faithful and competent servant, and he thought that, compared with others in the employ of the Corporation, Mr. Madeley was underpaid. They could not expect to get skilled services without paying a proper price, and, if anything, Mr. Madeley was worse paid than officials who performed the same duties in other towns. The amount they were paying, if £250, was extremely low for the services rendered. There was the Museum, the Library, and the Art Gallery, and Mr. Madeley had control of the three institutions. He also exercised certain control over the School of Art. They were now paying a gentleman £3OO a year for the work done by Mr. Madeley for £5O. Several Members: No, no._

Alderman BENNErr : It is substantially so. Mr. Madeley,he continued, had put in a great deal of labour in the matter of technical education, and whatever the success of it was there was no doubt that the foundation of secondary education had been laid by him. On that ground he was entitled to consideration. They were, in fact, paying him, for all his services, less than many head clerks received. Several MEMBERS No, no."

Alderman BENNETT : Thera are lawyer's offices in Warrington where the head clerks are receiving more than Mr. Madeley at the present time. it was alto- gether disproportionate to the amount of the services he had rendered. Although their-library was not ideal, and not what they would like to see it, that was no fault of Mr. Madeley's but through his not having suffi- cient funds to bring it up to modern requirements. The whole question had arisen out of the fact that in a town of 60,090 inhabitants the books had got soiled. How they could expect a democracy to keep books without soiling them, it would pass the wit of man to say. Mr. Madeley, at any rate, had done his best. They knew that in two or three departments they could com- pare favourably with many other towns in the country. With the scanty resources at his disposal he had done his best, and would do the work with any man in England if he were given more resources. He was held by his brother librarians in the highest res- pect, and had held some of the highest positions it was possible to hold. His opinions were greatly sought after by librarians and he was regarded as an authority. As to the Museum they knew that at least two or three departments would compare favourably with any in the country. The Art Gallery was not what they would like to see it, but with restricted means, Mr. Madeley had brought great ability and untiring diligence to pro- mote what really ought to represent the highest intel- lectual Hie of the town. If they were going to pay for it at the price of a head clerk it was disproportionate to what he was entitled to receive.

Councillor DODDS remarked that he had intended to give a silent vote upon the matter, as he had already stated his reasons for voting for the reduction of Mr. Madeley's salary. Alderman Monks was partly right in saying that at first it was a matter of procedure because it had been done in an irregular way. The resolution passed at the last meeting was, in effect, that as the duties for which he had been paid the extra £5O had been taken away Mr. Madeley's salary be forthwith reduced. That was the point which was raised really, and now they ought to have some reason given them for raising his salary to .2250 again. He did not think they ought to give him £5O because he had been having it, for some work he had done previously. He was pre- pared to face what he had done with his constituents. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Moncs said the committee brought it for- ward in February at the proper time in order to comply with the Standing Orders, and he thought they had done it in a way which had secured the approval of the Council. The Council certainly did approve and con- firm the minutes of the committee under which this money was paid to • Mr. Madeley, for a time. It was logical that having made a mistake they should take the earliest opportunity to put it right and get the matter in order,especially when it was doing a man an injustice. With regard to the amount of the salary, reference had ' been made to the fact that Mr. Madeley was paid more I than in other towns. That was not correct, as salaries
Of .£2OO, £250 and .£3OO were paid for the past of

omrian alone. Then in some towns £l5O or r. 200 were paid for the curator of the museum, and another £lOO or £2OO for the curator of the art gallery,making a total of £6OO or .2700 for the work that Mr. Madeley had been doino. for £2OO. A °VOICE: " QuestionN .
Councillor W. -ROBSRTS :_ Quitp. right.. (Laughter.)

Alderman MONKS continuing, said he only mentioned the matter as showing that Mr. liadeley, even taking into consideration the fact that the work of the Technical Institute had been taken out of his hands, had been paid a miserable sum for what he had been doing for the committee. With regard to what Alder- man Bennett had said as to the appreciation of his services in other towns, he knew that a successful attempt was being made to make a presentation to Mr. Madeley as an acknowledgment of what he had been able to-do for librarians generally in the north of England during the last few years. (Hear, hear.) It did not emanate from Warrington and was signed by the chief librarian of Liverpool, countersigned by a similar oificial at Manchester, and supported by the librarimis of the five northern counties. Even if Mr. Madeley did not do another stroke of extra work that money was due to him for the untirirg and zealous labour he had done in connection with the development of the Technical Schools. He had no hesitation in saying that apart from two or three members of the Council, no one had the slightest idea of the time, thought and work Mr. Madeley had put into technical instruction during the past twelve years. There was no doubt that whatever success attended the technical schools in the future would be due to Mr. Madeley. That alone entitled him to an advance. They were prepared to give him an ad- vance about three years ago, and it was a question whether he should not be appointed director of second- ary education, in which case he would probably have had an extra .£l5O, and not merely the £5O which they now proposed to give him in respect of the work hehad done. He was quite certain thatany reasonably-minded man would feel that it was a reasonable amount to pay, and he hoped the Council would agree to it. The amendment that the minutes of the Museum Committee be confirmed with the exception of the minute relating to the salary of Mr. Madeley was then put with the following result : For the amendment Councillor Dodds

• The usual monthly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held in the Board Room at the Work- house on Wednesday morning. Mr. A. Brooks presided and there were also present :—Mrs. Clay, Rev. Father Wilson, Dr. Murray, Messrs. T. H. Ashcroft, J. Clarke, J. W. Knowles, J. Payton, S. Davies, A. J. .Tolley, G. Mather, William Houghton, J. Turton, A. Jolley, G. • Pilling, J. Ball, Wm. Hickman, with Mr. J. C. Sutton (clerk). Mr. F. Gate (master), Mr. A. Wright (superin- tendent Padgate Schools). THE MASTER AND MATRON APPOINTED. I The House Committee reported that after considering the 63 applications for the position of master and matron the following were selected, viz.: Mr. and Mrs. • Aubery, Southwell ; Mr. and Mrs. Berry, Chorley • Mr. and Mrs. Carrington, Banbury; Mr. and Mrs. Fielding, ' Louth • Mr. and Mrs. Olsen, Cheadle. Messrs. Brooks and Pilling were deputed to visit each of the candi- dates and select three to appear before the Board. As a result of their visits Mr. and Mrs. Aubery and Mr.and Mrs. Carrington were invited to attend the Board meeting. . _

' Afteiinterviewing the candidates Mr. KNOWLES pro- posed that Mr. and Mrs. Aubery be appointed. Mr. Aubery he said, appeared to be a strong-minded man, and it was a man who could hold his own in the dis- charge of his duties that they wanted. If he had said he was a teetotaller—although he (Mr. Knowles) was not himself—it would have gone one further with him. (Laughter.) Mrs. CLA.Y seconded the proposition, Mr. A. JOLLEY supported, and it was carried unanimously. Mr AUBERY was then called into the room and in- formed of his appointment. He thanked the Board very much for the honour. There was no doubt they were coming to a house that had a reputation in England. They had been used to smaller houses for five or six years and would find the administration and responsi- bilities more difficult, but their best energies and ser- vices would be at the disposal of the Board. He felt sure if they showed they were trying to do their level best they would have the Board's sympathy and en- couragement. (Applause.) Mr. and Mrs. Aubery, the new masterand matron, who are 30 years of age are at present masterand matron of Sonthwell Workhouse. Prior to going to Southwell they were master and matron at Uttoxeter.

div.head: POOR LAW CONFERENCE,
div.p: THE POOR LAW CONFERENCE,

On the proposition of "Mr. decided that the Chairman, vice-chairman and Mr. Ashcroft attend the preliminary meeting of the North-Western Poor Law Conference to be held on 20th July at the Town Hall, Manchester.

div.head: ELECTRIC LIGHT PLANT,
div.p: THE ELECTRIC LIGHT PLANT,

The House Committee recommended that the Clerk communicate with the Chairman of the Corporation Electric Lighting Committee saying the Guardians would esteem it a very great favour if he wouldpermit Mr. Grimsdale to advige the Guardians respecting their electric-plant.

div.head: LOAN FOR. THE EXTENSION OF LAUNDRIES.
div.p: THE LOAN FOR. THE EXTENSION OF LAUNDRIES.

_ On the proposition of Mr. PILLING, seconded by Mr. A. J. JOLLEY, the seal of the Board was ordered to be attached to the deed securing repayment to the Public Works Loan Board of £2,225 and interest at £3 ss, per cent. for the extension of laundries, and to the certifi- cate authorizing payment of the loan to the union treasurer. THE ALTERATIONS TO THE VAGRANT CELLS.

Mr. PILLING moved and Mr. A. JOLLEY seconded a resolution consenting to the making of additions to the casual wards at the Workhouse of the Union, "in accordance with a plan to which the Local Govern- ment Board have affixed their seal, subject nevertheless to such modifications thereof as that Board may here- after direct; ani to the expenditure for the above pur- pose of a sum not exceeding £595, in lieu of a sum of £275, sanctioned by the Local Government Board on the 17th day of February,l9o3, to be expended for that purpose." Mr. G. MATHER inquired why the cost was going to be over £5OO when the estimated cost was only £275. Mr. GATE explained that the original plans were for 41 ineh walls between each cell, but it was found neces- sary to increase the width to 9in. It was also found that the hoppers would cost much more than estimated. The CHAIRMAN pointed out that before the tenders were opened, the architect admitted he had made a' mistake in the original estimate with regard to the vagrant cells, but on the other hand the tenders for the wash-houses were under the estimate, so that the cost of the wash-houses and vagrant cells would together amount to the architect's estimate.
Mr. HICKMAN remarked that the contract was for £560 and they were asking for £595. The CHAIRMAN said they were allowing something for architects commission.
The resolution was then passed. This was all the business of public interest.

Walking Day Arrangements. The Corporation have made the usual order with regard to street traffic on Walking Day. No cart, carriage, tramcar, lurry or any other vehicle (except lurries or other vehicles used fur conveying children in the procession, and mail carts, and no horse shall be allowed to remain in or travel along any of the following street between the hours of 9 a.m. and 12.30 p.m., viz: Arpley-street, Bewsey-street, Bold- street, Bridge-street, Buttermarket-street, Cairo-street, Church-street, Gol borne-street, Horsemarket-street, Irlam-street, Legh-street, Mersey-street, Parker-street, Rolleston-street, Sankey-street, Scotland-road, Wilson- Patten-street, and Winmarleigh-str eet. The order ceases to apply as soon as the procession, in its proper order, has passed along any of the streets named. Sharp-street Mission. With thu object of removing an adverse balance which has accumulated in connection with Sharp- street Primitive Methodist Mission, a sale of work was opened in the Mission Room on Tuesday after- noon, to raise funds- to liquidate the debt.—Mr. Griffiths, who presided, spoke of the importance and necessity of the work in that neighbourhood, and said it was very desirable that they should have a room of their own for worship, instead of having to pay rent. --Mrs. Armitage, in declaring the sale open, said there was plenty of work to be done, and hoped the sale would be successful.—On the motion of the Rev. J. Calvert, seconded by Mr. Bridge, and supported by the Rev. J. G. Reed, Mrs. Armitage was cordially thanked. The stalls were prettily arranged and pre- sided over by the following :—Fancy and clothing stalls, Mesdames Branwood, Meachin, Thompson, Elwell, and Boardman ; refreshment stall, Mesdames Parkes and Bridge. During the evening Miss Alice Bridge efficiently sang "The Stuttering Sweetheart." —The day's sales realised nearly £lO.
