So far, it Was added, nothing of quite the same kind has been attempted among members of the Opposi- tion; but "it is understood that:such inquiries as have been made have revealed a hitherto unsuspected amount of support:for the new idea among the :Radicals, many of whom, especially "long the business men, show themselves less, disnosed to pledge themselves irrevocably to the present fiscal system." Much of this, it is csbrious, is the latest from a more or less fertile imagination, working upon casual and probably humorous observations. We are in a position to State, with more authority, the real view of Radi- cal and Unionist members concerning Mr. effAxnEaLairr's latest schism. There has, to use Lord RoSEBERY'S expression, been no" diagonal 81'4 " in the Liberal party, which is perfectly 'ound as to Free Trade. We suspect that our London evening contemporary had overheard an Observation by a not very important member of ?ornament, who has large interests in South Africa. It will not be very alarming if" the l'ew ideas "—which are not* new and which have hardly yet taken the form of ideas— Should detach one member from the Liberal But what is the position of the Conservatives, and :those . who still continue to ce.ll themselves Unionists? We know, to some extent, what is the position of those who are mem- bers of the Government. The soundest minds bY which we mean those who have not only the 'tiost complete knowledge of social and economic 'questions, but those who have been continuously recognised on which ever side they might chance to sit as having a title to speak first,and with most decisiveness, on just such questions as this which has now arisen—the soundest minds in the oovernment, we repeat, not merely declare them- selves to be Free 'Traders, but affirm that any Wide departure from our present fiscal system Would not only injure the Empire, but would very Probably destroy it. It is true, no doubt, as our evening con- elnporary states, that efforts are being made to leduce members sitting on the Government side Of the House to declare whether they arelfor or algoinst Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. Mr. CFIAMBP.RLAIN Ftlnuelf may be trusted to spare no effort to 4d Out as speedily as possible who is for and ho is against him. He has 'placed the nation Ibu the position of the Trojan youth choosing tetween the goddesses. He is like her of whom NONE complained "that uninvited came tit,l_to the fair peleian banquet hall and cast he golden fruit upon the board, and bred this !lange." Members on the Liberal side are °t called upon to consider their position. 111e37 are Free Traders. And they are Free ,traders for the :same reason RS 14 Mr. RITCHIE' oltley are conscious of the vast Ejadvantages tee Trade."' But'on the Conservative benches IvisN are many members who, if Ithey are not of t".l3lLroun's temper of mind, have Mr. ALrotries freedom from conviction. They7will TeLtetroine nothing for themselves for the present. will wait to see how the leaven works ; they jump as the cat jumps; they really need not u,sricorn us for the present. beyond mere political opportunists, who w°llld rather be in Parliament on any terms than

out of it because they had adhered to even the most genuine of their convictions, there are two distinct pa:ties on the Ministeria benches. There are the convinced Protec- tionists and there are the convinced Free Traders . There must sooner or later be a separation —we do not like to say of the sheep from the goats—of those who study national and Imperial questions from the point of view of the general advantage, and those 'whose 'view of economic questions is bounded by their knowledge of the incidents of a particular trade or industry. If the separation is:not soon rather than late, the convinced Free Traders on the Tory side will find that the COLONIAL SECRETARY has stolen a march 'Ton them, cind that he has obtained such a lead that they cannot:overtake him. Their best policy, and one that they cannot adopt at too early a moment, is to.throw in their lot with all other Traders. The next election will then be fought on Free Trade, as the last election was fought on the war; and thus the nation, if it decides to ruin itself, will ac least be saved from ruining itself by dissensions.

SIR 11. CAMPBELL- interpellation was BANNERMAN'S MOTION ever more amply FOR ADJOURNMENT justified than that

of Sir HENRY CAMPBELL BANNERMAN 01. Wednesday night. The leader of the Liberal Party in the House of Coin- mons was compelled to take the strong step of mov- ing the adjournment in orthr to elicit from the Government a simple ite n of inforaratioa con- cerning its proposed course of action in con - nection with the singular misconception into which the PICEMIER. of New South Wales has permitted himself to bs betrayed by the recent speeches of Mr. BALFOUR and M. CHAMBERLAIN. It is a remarkable and inoit enlightening story that: has to be told. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is, for the time being, supposed to be tongue-tied on the subject of his " new ideas " but he is somehow contriving to pro3are strong pronouncements on his side from leading men in the colonies. First of all we had Mr. RICHARD SEDDJN Cabling his support, and then threatening to make reciprocal arrangements with the foreigner—a thing which, by the way, he has no power to do without the consent and assistance, of the mother country. Then Sir HARRY RAWSON the Governor of New South Wales, cabled over to express the satisfaction of the G var n men t of that country with the declaration by the British Government that every self-governing Colony shall be secured in the free exercise of its right to enter into the closer :tride relations with the mother country. This puzzled everybidy but the Colonial Secretary, who immediately had the message con- veyed to the Press, but declined to say a single explanatory word on the subject. We do Mr. BALFOUR the justice of believing that he was as much bewildered in the first instance as the public at large. He stated that he did not know what declaration was referred to. Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN sat by his side listening, and said nothing; but the fact that he had sent out the message from New South Wales is proof beyond all questioning that he wished the Colonies to believe that a specific declaration has been made by the Government of the kind spoken of by Sir HARRY RAWSON. He could have put Mr. BALFOUR right if he had chosen to do so. He could have telegraphed to New South Wales to say that there had been no declaration by the Government. Ile could have withheld from the Press a message which was obviously based on a mistake. But that was no part of his plan. Aay of these pro- ceedings wouli, in fact, have been wholly opposed to his idea of how his present campaign is to be conducted. He permitted the Government of New South Wales to remain under its delusion, and led the public at: home to believe that the declaration spoken of in Sir HARRY RawsoN's message had actually been made by the Ministry. It was open to Mr. BALFOUR, in the silence of the Colonial Secretary, to say in downright terms that there had been no "declaration," that the New South South Wales Government had made a , very serious mistake, and that he would lose no time in rectifying its error. But his mind is too tortuous for this straightforward manner of pro- ceeding. When he was questioned in .!•,he House of Commons, he merely fenced with his question ers, and when he was further questioned he obviously prevaricated. The hypothesis by which he , accounted on Tuesday for the New South Wales ' message was not merely preposteroes, but inex- cusable. It was, in an expressive slang phrase, "playing it low down "—almost as low down as it 'is possible to get. He suggested that the mes- sage referred to a declaration made by Lord SALISBURY so long ago fie 1897, when the late Prime Minister denounced the Treaties with Germany and Belgium. He said that " the object is to remove a barrier against the internal fiscal arrangement of the British E.npire." Six years latere,the present Premier has the amazing effron- tery to suggest to the House of Commons that a cable message from New South Wales is a reply to , this declaration of Lord SALISBURY. As if the ' Government of the Colony had never met for six lyears past, and had only just awakened to the necessity of replying to an ancient: declaration of la statesman who is no longer engaged in active political life! This manner of playing with great questions, which is peculiar to Mr. BALFOUR, has resulted, as it deserved to result, in a singular and humiliat- ing exposure. A London newspaper telegraphs to the Premier of New South Wales to inqu ire, as the Government should have done, what declar- ation was referred to, and gets for a reply the words: "Speeches delivered by CHAMBERLAIN and BALFOUR." The Colonies cannot understand that we have a Ministry without capacity for joint action, and without a sense of common responsi- bility. What is said by leading members of the Government they take, RS is but natural, as a Government " declaration." When they awaken to the true sense of the :situation, 'what will be the state of feeling in which they will find themselves? Contempt and anger must most certainly predominate. This is the great danger of Mr. OnameeßLArreslmethods of campaigning. They are -calculated, not to draw the Colonies closer.to the mother country, but to make them despise British statesmanship, and therefore to estrange them. The incisive and dignified speech of Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN on Wednesday night was not a whit too strong for the occasion. Ministers are not only playing with Parliament but they are deceiving the "British dominions beyond the seas." The end of such a proceeding we shall not see for a long time to come; but it , can hardly be otherwise thau disastrous.

The Examiner Friday, June, 19, 1903.

The pioneers in what is called the women's movement have little affection for Sir William ' Anson, and will probably have still less whon there has been time to ponder over an answer he has just given to a question on the subject of the working of the Education Act. It is expressly stated in one of the clauses of that measure that provision is to be made for the inclusion of women as well as men among the members of each Education Committee. Yet, on having brought to his notice the fact that in a number of schemes which have been approved there is provision for the presence of one woman only, Sir William Anion contends that these fully comply with the Jaw. To an ordinary mind " women" would seem to imply more than one. It is the common-sense understanding of the clause that at least two should be appointed. However, the Board of Education has certainly the interpreta- tion Act of 1889 to fall back upon, in which it is laid down that where it is not repugant to the whole sense of a clause the plural number should be held to include the singular, and where the singular number is used the law should equally apply to the plural number. It is an ingenious plea, and yet it can hardly be expected to satisfy fully the advocates of women on public repre- sentative bodies. The whole idea of the Inter- pretation Act is to widen the application statutes, and to prevent any evasion of obligations by mere quibbling about words. This, is, perhiips, the first occasion on which this clause has been used in oruer.to restrict and limit the meaning of an Act of Parliament.

The programme for the visit of M. Loubet to these shores has now been practically settled, and the head of the French Republic should, provided our British climate consents for once to be respect- able, have a very enjoyabie —though, perhaps. rather tiring—time in England. The President will be met by his Majesty the King at Victoria Station on his arrival on July 6th,and will be enter- tained at dinner by his Majesty in the evening, Luncheon with the City Fathers at the Guildhall, the return dinner to the King at the French Em- bassy, and the gala performance at the Opera will occupy the second day ,of the visit; and on the third M. Loubet will go to Aldershot to witness a review. This is an unexpected item in the arrangements, but none the less welcome, because it will let not only M.Loubet, but all those who accompany him, and the French people generally—through their news- papers—see for themselves something of the British Army which fought in South Africa under one of the foremost commanders in that campaign not the least reviled on the Continent, and appro- priately on this occasion, named Fcench. It is a curious reflection that the head of the French nation which three years ago was receiving Mr. Kriiger with acclamation should in July be the guest of the King at a review of the troops whose deeds were painted in such false and forbidding colours while the Boor war was progressing. After the review M. Loubet will dine with Lord Lans- downe. A great deal was made of the significance of the King's presence at the dinner table of the French Foreign Minister, M Delcassii during his visit to Paris, and it was generally surmised that international relations were not unconnected with the event. Lord Lansdowne's dinner, besides giving symmetry to the whole proceedings, is an indication that the French President's visit is not without its practical side.

In our correspondence column Mr. A. H. Lee calls attention to the importance of sending poor children into the country for a pprtion of their holidays, and appeals for assistance in the excel- eat work which he has for so long personally carried out in this direction. Mr. Lee has, for more than ten years, been sending 100 boys each year to the summer camp at Birkdale, and his idea is that thc scheme should be made a matter of public concern, and extended so as to embrace a number of boys more in proportion to the poor population of the town. It is thought that at least 400 children should be sent away for a week at a time, and to do this not only are more funds required, but a representative committee is neces- sary. We believe Mr. Lee will have little difficulty in getting this Committee together, for there are plenty of sympathisers with the poor, who should be glad to find such an outlet for their charity. We have already a Poor Children's Christmas Treat Committee in Warrington,and some of the same individuals might turn their hands and hearts to Mr. Lee's estimable project. It is of considerably greater importance than the Christmas treat, and we wish it well.

div.head: PASSIVE RESISTANCE.
div.p: PASSIVE RESISTANCE.
THE RECTOR OF WARRINGTON AND THE RESISTERS.

The RECTOR of Warrington (Rev. Canon Willis) preached at St. Barnabas' Church on Sunday evening at the concluding service of the patronal festival. The offertory was in aid of the Day and Sundny School funds and in appealing for liberal contributions the Rector said the present was a great crisis. They were told that crises were always taking place but nobody doubted that the present was a very trying time. There was a feeling that the church schools were being put more and more into the hands of the clergy and there was a disposition on the part of some to resent that. If they would only think care- fully and seriously they would see that the Education Act instead of putting the schools more into thQ power of the clergy was putting them less in that power than they were before. Previously the incum- bent might rule in the dayschools, but he could not do so now. There were four foundation managers and two representative managers, and the clergyman had but a voice. His voice carried great weight if his people res- pected and loved him, but there was not a one man management—anything but that. Those who were sup- posed to be extreme or advanced men instead of court- ing the Act and feeling pleased, were the ones who dis- liked it most; not because they wanted to have the power, but because they loved their children and wanted to bring them up in the tree faith—to give them the very best secular education that was possible, and at the same time the very best religious education too. They were told that some people were upholding passive resistance. They said it was against their con- sciences to pay the rates. It had never been against their consciences to pay the imperial taxes so why should it be against their consciences to pay the rates? Then again it had never been against the consciences of Churchpeople —though they had disliked it very much—to pay to- wards the support of the Board schools, and there had never been any passive resistance. Churchmen had never hesitated to pay towards the maintenance of Board Schools, even though it was against what they believed to be right. The clergy valued the day schools simply because they wanted to teach the children what they knew to be right. Let them think of the importance of being able to teach the truths of their religion during the first hour of five days in every week. No Sunday school could ever equal it and that was why they were so anxious to re- tain their schools. It would, however, he a difficult thing to do so. They had been relieved of a great deal of the expenses—the payment of the salaries of the teachers—but the cost of repairs,extensions,and mainte- nance of the schools would still fall upon Church people Where they were to get the money from it was difficult to see. He appealed to them for liberal contributions to the school funds of that parish. WILLESDEN COUNCIL'S OFFER TO PASSIVE

RESISTERS. —"The Rates Department of the Willesden District Council, acting on counsel's opinion, has decided to accept a portion of the poor-rate less the voluntary school part.—The department has also agreed to take instalments of the rate, but will only give a receipton account of the whole sum demanded—not for a sec- tional part. The citizens' league of 'passive resistance therefore refuses to pay. 'WIDNES FREE CHURCHMEN.

On Tuesday evening a largely-attended meeting Was held at Widnes, under the 'auspices of the Local Preach- ers' Council, to protest against the action of the Town Council in refusing fair representation of the Noncom formists on the new Education Committee. The Rev. A. liarvey presided. Sympathetic messages of encour- agement were received from Dr. Clifford and Mr. Lloyd George.—Vigorous speeches were made by the chair- man and Mr. Jones (Liverpool), Mr. Gawtrev (St. Helens), the Rev. A. Jones, and the Rev. J. Pedlar, strongly advocating the adoption of the passive resist- ance movement in Widnes.—A resolution was passed regarding with the greatest indignation the action of the majority of the Town Council in rejecting the nomination of Mr. E. Thomas from the Education Committee, and condemning the rejection of Council- lors George Davies and David Lewis.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. The Infected Blankets at Grappenhall. STOCKTON HEATH'S REPRESENTATION.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. The Infected Blankets at Grappenhall. STOCKTON HEATH'S REPRESENTATION.
The monthly meeting of the aboce Council was held on Tuesday morning at Duttou.—.4r. S. Woodward presided.
SPECIAL EXPENSES.

A communication was received from the Local Government Board, enclosing copies of an order declar- ing the remuneration payable to the Clerk and Surveyors in connection with the Parochial Committees of the district to be special expenses, chargeable upon each contributory place.
INFECTED SOUTH AFRICAN BLANKETS AT ORAPPENHALL.

A letter from the Local Government Board intimated that some of the South African blankets had been sent by a London firm to Grappenhall,and that"bacteriological examination had shown that some of them were probably specifically infected." They advised that such blankets should be steamed and washed, or else destroyed altogether; and asked for a report on the matter by the Medical Officer of Health.

Dr. Adams reported that the Clerk had notified him of the blankets that had been sent to the Rural District. It appeared that only six blankets had been sent to Grappenhall as samples, one of which had been bought by a police officer and the rest returned. He had obtained the blanket at a cost of 28. 9d., and it had been destroyed.

div.head: THELWALL NUISANCE.
div.p: THE THELWALL NUISANCE.

The Clerk to the County Council wrote as follows on June 4th with regard to the alleged effluvium nuisance at Thelwall :—I submitted a print of Professor Delapine's report upon the alleged nuisance complained of by Mr. Nayloras arising from Messrs Long's tannery in your rural district to the Public Health Committee of this Council at its last meeting when I Was instructed to forward a copy of such report to Mr. Naylor with an intimation that the Council was satis- fied therewith and did not propose to take any further action upon his complaint and this I have already done. The Chairman: I presume that is satisfactory to you as a Rural District. The Clerk in reply to further questions stated that the report had been sent to the Local Government Board but no reply had yet been received.

div.head: AMALGAMATION SCHEME.
div.p: THE AMALGAMATION SCHEME.

The County Council forwarded notices of the forth- coming inquiry to be held at Runcorn on June 23rd, concerning the proposed extension of the Runcorn Urban boundaries to include the parishes of Halton and Weston.
There was no report from the Committee appointed to deal with the matter.
TELEPHONE AND TELEGRAPH POLES IN THE RURAL DISTRICT.

Admiral Jones-Parry raised the question asked at the last meeting whether poles in the Rural District should be compulsorily painted white eight feet from the ground and rambling discussion ensued in which the Clerk stated that the County Council had not decided to make it compulsory to have the poles so painted. Ultimately it was resolved that the telephone and tele- graph companies be approached to ascertain whether they would agree to paint the poles in such a manner.

div.head: DRAINAGE QUESTION.
div.p: A DRAINAGE QUESTION.

The Farnham Rural District Council forwarded the following resolution and hoped the council would pass a similar one and forward it to the Local Government Board: That it is urgently necessary thatpowers should be conferred upon all rural district Councils altogether to prohibit the building of dwelling houses upon sites so low-lying and water-logged as to be absolutely un- suitable for the purpose and a constant source of danger to the health of the district; also that in rural dis- tricts where there is no system of drainage rural district councils should be empowered to require an open space suitable for the disposal upon it of the domestic sewage arising from the house of at least 1000 square feet to be provided in connection with each new dwelling house. On the motion of Mr. Linaker it was resolved that the letter lie on the table,ithe Inspector remarking that if the Farnham Council adopted the model buildings bye-laws that would settle the question.

div.head: BELLPIELD COMPLAINT.
div.p: THE BELLPIELD COMPLAINT.

Mr. \V. H. Woodcock, borough collector, who wrote on May 23rd intimating that nothing had been done res- pecting the nuisance near Bellfield said he would be glad to see the matter pushed forward. Mr. Swinton, surveyor, said that he visited the place on the sth inst and there was no nuisance whatever.

div.head: MUNICEPAL OFFICERS ASSOCIATION. _
div.p: THE MUNICEPAL OFFICERS ASSOCIATION. _

The Municipal Officers Association forwarded circular letters and other matter which had beenaddressed to members of Parliament, with a view to furthering the progress of the Local Authorities' Officers' (Adoptive) Superannuation Bill, and asked the Council to use their influence in the matter with the local members of Par- liament. The Council decided to ask the local members to support the Bill, as a similar resolution had already been passed by them supporting the aim and provisions of the measure.

div.head: ISOLATION HOSPITAL SCHEME.
div.p: THE ISOLATION HOSPITAL SCHEME.

Mr. Woodward, Chairman of the Isolation Hospital Cemmittee, reported that a fortnight ago the plans and detailed specifications of the above hospital had been laid before the Committee, who had unanimously approved them. He therefore proposed that the plans be passed by the Council, and that they be sent to the Local Government Board with a request for a loan of £6,000 for the erection of the building. Mr. Linaker seconded.
The Chairman explained that the site had already been purchased, and that the money would equip thehospital in every particular for immediate use. The Council approved the report unanimously.

div.head: RELSB Y SEWERAGE.
div.p: RELSB Y SEWERAGE.
The seal of the Council was affixed to an additional loan of £lB7O on account of the Helsby sewerage on the motion of Messrs. Collier and Stokes. STOCKTON HEATH'S REPRESENTATION ON THE COUNCIL.

Mr. Pilling, chairman of the committee appointed to deal with the above question, said that the committee had agreed that there was no evidence to justify a petition to the County Council asking for increased representation for Stockton Heath. They found that there were other districts in a similar position. The Council approved the committee's report.

div.head: ADMIRAL PARRY'S BRIEF.
div.p: ADMIRAL PARRY'S BRIEF.

Admiral Parry drew attention to the fact that the Clerk under the head of other letters had not read one from Mr Naylor. Had one been received? Mr. Naylor had written to him stating that he intended writing on Professor Delapine's report.

The Clerk safd he had received such a letter from Mr Naylor but had replied to it. It was to the effect that he trusted the Council would permit him to lay his views personally before them. The Clerk had written pointing out that the matter was yet in the hands of the Local Government Board. The Clerk'a action was approved.

div.head: COMMON PIT.
div.p: COMMON PIT.

Mr. Guest stated that he had visited the pit and had ascertained that the landlord was responsible for the erection of the fence. He suggested, therefore, that Mr. C. Evans be written to requesting the fence to be erected and that a copy of the Coroner's letter be en- closed.
Mr. Stokes seconded, and the resolution was approved.

THE NORTH-WESTERN ELECTRIC GAS AND POWER BILL. Mr. Linaker stated that the Parliamentary Committee had resolved to oppose some of the clauses in the Bill. The committee had endeavoured to obtain from the promotersl concessions respecting the liability of the road sections in the Bill. They wanted them to insert clauses so that the company would be liable for damage to Rural District roads, as well as County roads. The Rural Council, too, was responsible .if the pipes were in any way damaged if they were two feet six below the snrface of the road. the Rural Council would not be in a position to fight such clauses before the House of Commons Committee, unless they took necessary steps by instructing the Council. was essential that the road should be pro- tected.
Mr. P illling seconded, and the Council adopted the Committee's report.
FINANCE. Mr. Wright reported that there was a balance in hand of £9OB 16s. 4d.
THE HOSPITAL.

Mr. P. Gleave drew attentioni to the fact that the hospital had only one exit, and that in case of fire the inmates would be placed in a most dangerous position. He thought there should be two emergency doors placed in the men's and women's wards.
Dr. Adams supported this view, andpointed out where the doors could be placed. It was resolved that two extra doors be provided, and that certain minor repairs be executed.

div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
NEW POST OFFICE OFFICIAL.
Mr. R. Moore has resigned the sub-postmastership of Delph Bridge office, Runcorn, and has beensucceeded by Mr. James 0, Sherratt.
DROWNED AT SEA.

The steamship Grampus belonging to Mossrs. G. and J. Burns, from Glasgow to Manchester touched at Run- corn on Friday afternoon when Captain Blair reported that when passing Pladda buoy on Thursday night a passenger named Mather Warburton fell overboard and was drowned. ' RUNCORN LIBRARY REPORT.

div.head: SAD END OF "FISH TOM."
div.p: SAD END OF "FISH TOM."

At the Runcorn Police Court, on Friday, Mr.Dobson, coroner, inquired into the circumstances attending the death of Thomas Smith (Fish Tom) of 10, Green-street. The evidence showed that for some time deceased had been an object of charity as he was an old man of seventy and could not do any work. He earned a poor living byselling oranges. Deceased was last seen alive on Tuesday and on Wednesday morning inquiries were mtde about him by Thomas Steele and Mrs. Jones as he was known to be in a precarious state of health. He was then found behind the door quite dead, the house be- ing in a very dirty condition. The medical evidence showed that the bag of the heart contained a large clot of blood which was accountable for his death. A ver- dict in accordance with Dr. MacLennan's evidencewas returned.

div.head: SHOCKING NEGLECT Or CHILDREN.
div.p: SHOCKING NEGLECT Or CHILDREN.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. J. Ockleston (in the chair) and Mr. A. R. Norman, Albert Ravenscroft,l9, Wyvern-place, Runcorn, was charge/ with neglecting his five children, John, Albert, Leonard, Ernest and Fred, in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering and injury to health. The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. F. Johnson) said the case was adjourned from two or three weeks ago in order to afford the prisoner an opportunity of improving the con- dition of his home. Prisoneragain pleaded not guilty.— The evidence showed that Superintendent and Sergeant Cooper visited the prisoner's house on Saturday after nine o'clock. The doors were locked and two little children were crying in the kitchen. The mother was away and prisoner was found in a public house. There was no food save a bit of butter in the house. Later the mother came in with some potatoes stating that prisoner had only given her Is. to buy food with.— Inspector Hackett said there had been practically no improvement since the adjournment.—Prisoner stated he could not get work and went to the public-house to play on the piano and get some money. He was com- mitted for 6 months hard labour. A TRUANT SENT AWAY. - • '

At the Runcorn Veit:i.-S•:;s--siOn;-nn- -Monday, Patrick Kilkenny, labourer, Fryer-street, was summoned for not sending his son James to school. He stated that the boy was beyond his control. Mr. Lightburn (clerk to the school Board) said he had made arrangements for the boy's admission to an industrial school. The lad was then charged with being found wandering and not under proper control. Messrs. Bowyer and Howard, school attendance officers, said they had repeatedlyseen the lad about the streets. The father had been summoned for him nine times and had been before the committee 38 times. The father was sworn and stated that he went to work early in the morning and could not see the lad to school. He could not manage him. The lad was ordered to the Bishop Browne school at Stockport until the age of 16 with two years' supervision to follow, and the father was ordered to pay 2s. weekly towards his maintenance.
LOCAL WILLS : MRS. HAZLEHURST AND MR. W. ROWLANDS.

By her will, dated 2nd February, 1896, Mrs. Julia Hazlehurst, of Halton Grange, Runcorn, who died on 11th January last, aged 71 years, widow of Mr. Charles Hazlehurst,appointed as executors,her son, Mr. Charles Whiteway Hazlehurst,of Moreton Court,Hereford,and her friend Mr. Joseph Hall Salkold,of Runcorn, estate agent by whom her estate has been valued at .£0,245 12s. 9d. gross,and at £8,236 14s. 2d. net. Mr. William Rowlandpf Eversley, Runcorn, and of 9, Canning-place, Liverpool, ship-owner and carrier,who died onthe 4th May last,left estate of the gross value of £24,941 15s. 11d., with net personalty£ls,6Bs 13s. id. By his will of Ist February, 1894, with a codicil, he appointed as executrix and executors his wife Mrs. Jane Rowland, his son William Ernest Rowland, and Richard Hough, of Ways Green, to the last-named of whom he bequeathed £25, to his sons Ernest and Alfred each a gold watch and chain,and to Mrs. Rowland £lOO and the income of his residuary estate, which, subject to her interest, he left in trust as to one-tenth for his son Alfred, as to one-tenth for his daughter Annie wife of James Littler, and as to the remainder for his other children. The executrix and executors may retain the testator's shares in ships and continue his business to a company.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT].

While Widnesis violently exercising itself over the working of the new Education Act Runcorn has not yet escaped from the reactionary apathy of the last School Board victory. Why in the world the Runcorn Free Church Council is not "up and doing" its share in the passive resistance movement, with such nultant gentlemen as the Rev. Sydney Morris and Mr. Walter Millington at the head, passes my comprehension. Runcoan, is fast losing, if it has not already lost its reputation for being a go-arhead Radical town. Oppor- tunities for resisting the spread of clericalism are being thrown away, and local Nonconformity ought to be thoroughly ashamed of its supineness. Meanwhile those who cried loudest at the last School Board elec- tion are preparing, with sickly smiles,to pay the clerical tax. It is a wonder that the shades of our sturdy Non- conformist ancestors do not haunt us for betraying the trust reposed in us.

Considerable interest centres in the inquiry which will be held at the Runcorn Town Hall into the amalgamation petition of the Runcorn Urban Council. There seems to be a pretty confident opinion that the Urban authority will be able to show very good grounds for the absorption of Weston and that the absorption will actually take place. It is, too, anticipated, that the lower part of Halton will come 'in. At all events the Urban Council confidently expect they will get "something.,' There will be a grievous disappointment if the petition is entirely non-suited and corresponding jubilation by the Rural Council.

Mr. Naylor has asked the favour of a personal inter- view with the Rural Council re Prof. Delepine's report on the Thelwall Nuisance. The Local Government Board, however, has the matter still in hand, and pend- ing a reply Mr.Naylor's proposal cannot be entertained. When the report of the Local Government Board arrives the matter will be at an end so far as the Rural Council is concerned, and Mr.. Naylor must not be so foolish to suppose that the Council will then go out of its way to hear him. Mr. Naylor and his letters will be shelved for ever and a day. He has; as a matter of fact, had his last word, and he will he a very fortun- ate or unfortunate man if he succeeds in bearding the august lions in the den.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

Found Dead in Bed. About 1.15 a.m. on Tuesday, one of the lodgers in Kermode's lodging house, Rose and Crown-street,was found dead in bed. The deceased man was a stranger, but the previous evening he had given his name as James Mullins, and said he had come from Widnes.
ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL WATERS.—Advt.

lronmoulder's Suicide. An irnnmoulder named James Gregory, 63 years of age, residing at 4, Providence-place, committed suicide on Sunday afternoon His wife left home at 1.40 leaving deceased in the kitchen. On returning at 2.10 she went upstairs and found him hanging by a rope attached to a nail in the bedroom wall. A neigh- bour named William Fox was called in and deceased was cut down. Life was then extinct. For the past eight months deceased had suffered from severe pains in the head and had been very low spirited.—At the inquest on Tuesday a verdict of" Suicide whilst of unsound mind "was returned.

div.head: ST. JOHN AMBULANCE. ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ST. JOHN AMBULANCE. ASSOCIATION.
Runcorn Branch.

The annual meeting of the members of the St. John Ambulance Association (Runcorn Branch) was held in the Technical Institute on Thursday evening Mr. F. J. Norman (president) in the chair. The Treasurer, (Mr. W. Banks) submitted a report which showed a balance in hand of £2 16s. Id.—The report of the Secretary(Mr. Greeory)showed that there had been 52 candidates for examination of whom 47 had satisfied the examiner.

An interesting address was given by the Chairman after which certificates were distributed to the following : Arthur Hopwood. William Hearn, Bernard Gibbs,. Wm. Gleave, Joseph Faulkner, Thomas Eagle, Alex. Elliott, Henry Dobson, Robert Davies, Henry sins, George Coulfield, George Bowman, Thomas P. Baxter, Wm. H. Jarvis, James Joyce, S. Lane, Ernest Lee, Wm. S. Looker, Thomas .G Moore, Charles Moorfield, Herbert C. T. Jones, Joseph Newall, John J. Nield, Robert Owens, George Oultram, John Preston, Harry Pope, Wm. Peacock, John Peacock, Herbert J. Pendlebury, George Powell. Charles H. Richards, John L. Saunders, John G. Setterfield and Joseph Shaw (Ist year certifi- cates) ; W. Oakes, S. Booth and E. Brooker (2nd year certificates) ; W. Clare, R. Gibbs, W. Ford, R. Hughes, T. Carson, G. Cowley, J. Harrison, T. Murphy, and J. Leach (medallions).—The following officers were elec- ted: President, Mr. F. J. Norman; Mr. W. Banker, treasurer; Mr. W. Gregory. secretary; Committee, Messrs. R. Gibbs, G. Hill, H. J. Pendlebury, W. Booth, J. Nieid, W. Ford, R. L. Hughes, A. Steele, J. Newell, T. G. Moores, and W. Peacock • auditors, Messrs. J. Littler aud T. Inc,defield. Later Messrs. Bankes, Gregory, and G. Hill were the recipients of useful pre- sents for their work in connection with the Association.

div.head: WALKING GRAZE.
div.p: THE WALKING GRAZE.
At Runcorn.

The employees of the Highfleld Tanning Company, Limited,have arranged for a 20 mile walk on Saturday. There are 60 entries. The route will be from the tannery through Halton, Hallwood, Dutton, Stretton, Whitley, Stockton Heath to the Ship Canal Bridge, and back by Walton and Moore. A RUNCORN "WALKER."

Among the competitors in the walk front New Ferry to Llangollen on Saturday, promoted by the Liverpool shipping interest, was Mr. L. A. Meredith, of Runcorn, who is engaged in one of the Liverpool offices. He finished tenth in the contest, covering the distance, 37 miles, in 6hrs. 59min. 30secs.

div.head: TONSORIAL TRAMP TO WARRINGTON.
div.p: A TONSORIAL TRAMP TO WARRINGTON.

A walk, promoted by the Leigh, Tyldesley," Atherton, and District Hairdressers' Association took place on Tuesday. the course being Warrington and back, a distance of 21 miles. Of 32 entrants only about half put in an appearance at the starting point, where a large crowd had gathered. The route chosen was via Butts Bridge, Glazebury, Culeheth, and Padgate, the return journey being made through Winwick and Lowton. Of the competitors who were in the official list S. Brooks early established a good lead, but he was beaten by anon-competitor--a postmannamed Spedding —who eventually came in first in the time of 3hr. 45min. The result of the walk, however, was :-1, S. Brooks, 3hr. 56min.; 2, H. Hallows, 4hr. smin.: 3, T. Hope, 4hr. 6min. Eight others finished. The first three ye- ceive medals.

div.head: AN EARLESTOWN AUCTIONEER AND HIS COMMISSION.
div.p: AN EARLESTOWN AUCTIONEER AND HIS COMMISSION.
Action at the Warrington County Court.

Before his Honour, Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., at the Warrington County Court on Thursday, Gabriel Moon, auctioneer and estate agent, carrying on business at Earlastown claimed £29 10s. commission and £2 I2s for services rendered from James Gibson, of Medlock chemical works, Knott Mill, Mancliester, in connection with the sale of "The Woodlands," Newton-le-Willows, which formerly belonged to the defendant. Mr. Longton, solicitor, Warrington, represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Jordan, barrister, Manchester, appeared on be- half of the defendant

In stating the plaintiff's case, Mr. Longton observed that at the time the action arose the defendant was resident at the Woodlands, Newton-le-Willows. It was a large leasehold residence with extensive grounds and the defendant wanted to sell it. It was on sale for some considerable time and the defendant got into communication with the plaintiff who proceeded to negotiate for the purchase of it. The defendant told the plaintiffl that he was very anxious that, the sale should be carried out as soon as possible, and to the surprise of the plaintiff, asked him what his commission would be. The plaintiff had been in communication with several parties with the object of finding a purchaser, and of course the purchaser would pay a commission to the plaintiff. When the defendant asked him what he would charge as commission, Mr. Moon said he was acting for someone else but would charge him one per cent. The defendant replied that that was a very reasonable figure and expressed the hope that the plaintiff would get the transaction carried through. The transaction proceeded on the under- standing that Mr. Moon was to receive one per cent. commission if he introduced a customer. Mr. Moon went to a great deal of trouble in the matter and the ultimate result was that a purchaser was iritlroduced who secured the property for £2,950. In due course Mr Moon supplied a bill to the defendant for commission and£2 2s. forsome services rendered. The two guineas , had been paid into court. Some time afterwards the plaintiff called npon the defendant with reference to the bill, and the defendant did not repudiate his respon- sibility or deny that he owed the bill. He promised to deal with it in due course. Nothing was done in the matter andhe (Mr. Longton) was instructed to write to the defendant. No notice was taken of the first letter but on a second application being made, the defendant replied that he looked upon the request for payment as a species of blackmail and should treat it accord- ingly. Mr. Longton, continuing, said there was no doubt that the plaintiff introduced Colonel Pilkington as a purchaser, and although the plaintiff received a commission from Colonel Pilkington, that had nothing to do withithe distinct agreement made by the defend- ant to pay the plaintiff one per cent. commission. Gabriel Moon' the plaintiff, was then called and cor- roborated Mr. Longton's statement. Cross-examined by Mr. Jordan, witness admitted that on his own showing he was acting on behalf of Colonel Pilkington, and of course got paid by Colonel Pilking- ton. The telegram produced was sent by witness offering £2,750 for the property. On the 12th November, 1901, a contract was drawn up between witness, acting as agent for Colonel Pilkington, and the defendant, in which it was agreed that the purchase price should be £2950. Witness denied that the defendant treated him throughout the whole transaction as acting solely for Colonel Pilkington. It was Mr. Gibson who first hsked him with regard to commission.

Mr. Jordan submitted that on a point of law the plaintiff was out of court. The plaintiff's evidence as it stood, without any cross-examination or argument on his side, showed that the plaintiff whilst acting as agent for Colonel Pilkington also entered into an arrangement with the defendant as regarded commission on the sale of the house. He was in the position of agent for Colonel Pilkington where if he was to discharge his duty to Colonel Pilkington he had to get the property at as low a price as he• could, and he was also making out that he was acting as agent for Mr. Gibson and receiving a percentage on the purchase money, where it would be to his advantage to get as much as possible. He submitted that if the plaintiff was acting as agent for Colonel Pilkington he had no right of action against the defendant. The law would not tolerate any agreement of that kind. The law ill effect said that no man could serve two masters. Mr. Jordan procnded to quote authorities bearing out his contention.

His Honour said the defendant had used a most un- fortunate expression in describing the application for payment as blackmail. He wished to express his opinion that on the facts of the case put before him the expres- sion was wholly inapplicable to the plaintiff's con- duct.

Mr. Jordan said he agreed it was an unfortunate clx- pression. It was one of those stupid words which were put down in moments of irritation and bad temper. His Honour: It it an unfortunate expression. Mr. Moon has been quite open in his conduct, and whatever the result of the action, he comes out of it quite honourably.

Mr. Jordan said he denied the evidence given as to the promise of commission by the defandant. He was simply taking the plaintiff's own case and said the plaintiff could not succeed on a matter of law. He failed to see where any services on behalf of Mr. Gibson had taken place. Mr. Moon had been paid for any trouble he had taken by Colonel Pilkington. His Honour said his present inclination was legally in the defendant's favour, but he would like Mr. Gibson t'o be called. The defendant then entered the box and denied that during the negotiations for the sale of the property he promised Mr. Moon an extra commission of one per cent. He declined to have anything to do with him unless he told him for whom he was acting. At first Mr. Moon refused to tell him, but he returned shortly afterwards and said he was acting for Colonel Pilkington. In answer to his Honour, witness said that when the plaintiff visited him at Manchester, he expressed sur- prise to the plaintiff that he should send him a bill for commission. His Honour gave judgment for the defendant without costs.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
VIADUCT WORKS OFFICIALS PICNIC.

The office staff and foremen of above works had their annual picnic on Saturday last. The party left Earlestown in a special saloon for Kendal arriving there about 12.0. Lunch was immediately partaken of at the Commercial Hotel and afterwards a number drove to Levens Hall and inspected the house and beautiful gardens whilst others indulged in bowling and walks until dinner was served. The weather was beautifully fine during the whole of the day. Kendal was left at 7 30, the party reaching home at 11 30. EARLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE EMPLOYES ANNUAL

div.head: P 1 CN rc.
div.p: P 1 CN rc.

The employs of the Ea.rrestown Co-operative Society held their annual picnic on Wednesday. The party. num- bering 53 left Earlestown in waggonettes for Warring- ton at 5.45, leaving there at 7.0 and reaching their destination, Matlock-Bath at 10.45. A tour round the lead mines and the caverns was made by the party who then proceeded to dinner. Afterwards they drove to Chatsworth House and went through the Hall and grounds. After tea a short time was spent in looking round the town. A start was made for home at 8 o'clock, •Earlestown being reached at 11.30. The arrangements were admirably carried out by Mr. Onions. WARGRAVR CHURCH EARLESTOWN.

The 'annual services in aid of the day and Sunday schools connected with the Wargrave and 'Vulcan were held on Sunday in the above Church. At the morning service, the sermon was preached by the Rev. Morley Stevenson of Warrington, and in the evening by the Rev Canon Penrhyn, rector of Winwick. Special hymns were sung by tho children, and a solo was nicely given by Miss Ada Merritt. In the afternoon an organ recital was given before a fair congregation by Mr. E. Hardy of Manchester, and sacred items were sung by Mr. John Molyneux and the choir. Owing to the inclement weather, the congregations were not Large, and this affected the collections, which only amounted to a little over £B. 1.0.G.T. HOPE OF EARLESTOWN LODGE.

The weekly meeting was held on Monday, when a good programme was arranged by Miss E. Woods. Mr. G. Clarke presided, and the followiug items were very nicely rendered: Opening ode and prayer; solo, "Holy City," Master Fred k'inchall; recit, "The Dutchman's family," Mr. T. Huffer: solo, "Deane," Miss J. Hill; solo, "Tatters„' Miss E. Clarke; recit, "What the train brought," Miss Frith; solo, "Killarney," Master F. Finchall; Lancashire reading, Mr. G. Clarke; solo, "Fisherman and his child," Miss J. Hill; recit, "Unawares," Miss Frith. Mr. Bateman, of Warrington, also gave some very amusing imitations. Thanks were accorded to the friends who took part. A very pleasant evening was brought to a close by singing God be with you till we meet again," and the Benediction.

div.head: CHILD SCALDED TO DEATH.
div.p: CHILD SCALDED TO DEATH.

On Saturday, Mr. S. Brighouse, the county coroner, held an inquiry, at the Town Hall, Earlestown into the circumstances surrounding the death of Kate arlon,four years of age, residing with her parents at 11, Hazel- grove, Earlestown, who met her death by scalds.—Mrs. l‘laggie Carlon, mother of deceased, stated that on Tuesday the 9th inst., she was washing clothes and she had lifted a pan of hot water off the fire on to the kitchen floor. Deceased was then in the kitchen, and in the absence of her mother, who was getting a dolly-tub, she fell into the pan of water. Witness heard her daughter shout ".oh, mamma," and on turning round found her with the lower part of her body in the hot water. She at once took her out and stripped her of her clothes and ran into a neighbour's, who dressed the wounds. Dr. Valentine was sent for, and the following morning he attended the deceased, who was very seriously scalded all over the lower parts of the body. The child died on Friday.—ln answer to the Coroner, Mrs.Carlon said that it was a small washing pan. The deceased was insured in a society for a penny per week.—The jury returned a verdict of Accidental death."
NEWTON-LE-WILLOW S RAILW A Y STATION BUR GL ED

A daring robbery was enacted at Newton-le-Willows on Sunday, when the railway station booking office was broken into by burglars. A window was brokenand the catch was pushed back. After forcing and ransacking several drawers, they mist have been very disappointed, as the whole of the money taken during the day had been removed to the safe. On examination it was clearly seen that an attempt had been made to force the safe, but, owing probably to being disturbed, they abandoned their task. However, the Post Office mail bag, containing parcels and letters from Scotland and the North was discovered on the premises, and the marauders opened it and extracted the whole of the missives, which, after examination, were scattered in the waiting-rooms and on the line. The bag was after- wards thrown in the garden attached to the Legh Arms Hotel.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
TRA.MCXRS IN COLLISION.

About a quarter to eleven on Monday morning an alarming collision occurred in Church-street, St. Helens. Two tramcars, one proceeding to St. Helens Junction, and the other to Haydock, started from the Bridge- street terminus together. Near the Parish Church the Junction car, which was first, was drawing up when the other car, being close behind, ran into the hind part with considerable force. The back of the Junction car was broken, and the windows of the Haydock Car were smashed, the driver fortunately escaping the broken glass by dodging backwards. There were several passengers in both cars, but beyond experiencing the shock they were not injured. The Junction car was so much damaged that it had to be driven into the sheds. DRAWING ROOM MEETING.

On Tuesday afternoon a drawing room meeting was held at " Highfield "St. Helens, by the kindness of Mrs. Oppenheim, on behalf of the funds of the Police Court and Prison Gate Mission of the Liverpool Diocesan C.E.T.S.—Mr. H. S. Oppenheim, J.P., Town Clerk of Widnes, who presided, expressed his sympathy with the object of the meeting. The Mayor of St. Helens—Mr. F. R. IDixon Nfttall, J.P., was the first speaker. His Worship referred to the time when he was the Mayor eleven years previously, when a meet- ing was held in the town with the object of raising the necessary funds to engage a police court missionary,and that though the proposal received little support at the time, he expressed his certainty that the object was a worthy one, and his opinion had been strengthened,. for since that time a missionary had been working at the police courts with excellent results. Mr. T. E. Sampson, J.P., coroner of Liverpool, who was next speaker gave a number of instances when the police court missionary's work had been helpful at the courts over which he presided. The other speakers were the Revs. Gtnon Willink and J. Hirst (secretary) and Mr. C. E. Bingham, local police court missionary. The collection realized £6 ss. Tea and coffee were afterwards served on the lawn.

Another suicide occurred on Tuesday near the Clifton Suspension Bridge. A young lady was sitting on the seat at the summit of the rocks, when she suddenly. threw herself over the precipice, and, falling on her head on the rocks, was instantly killed. The body has not been recovered.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
Minor Cases.
Warrington Borough Police Court.
FRlDAY.—Before Mr. H. Roberts (in the chair), Alder- man Smethurst, Councillor John Roberts, Messrs Hep_herd and Thornton.

A.SIONTII FOR WIFE ASSAULT.—Thomas Rutter, 21, Naylor-street, was summoned for assaulting his wife Mary Alice Rutter, 12, Litton's Row, on Jtuie 7th—lir. Steel appeared for the complainant and said the parties had lived apart for sometime. On the date in question defendant forced his way into the house, made use of bad language and on being told to leave seized com- plainant by the throat and struck her several times about the head with his closed fist.—Defendant denied the assault.—He had previously been fined for asimilar 'offence and was now sentenced to a month's hard labour.

WIFE DESERTION.—AIbert Jackson 158, Liverpool road, was summoned for deserting his wife Mary Jackson, 4, Hesketh streat.—Mr. Browne defended—Com- plainant said her husband left her a fortnight ago and had not given her any money since he went away— Defendant said his wife told him to go away and he did so.—Ultimately defendant agreed to a separation order and he was ordered to pay 12s 6d per week alimony— Arthur Gleave, Chorley street, was summoned for deserting his wife Mary Elizabeth Gleave, 5, Peer's yard—Defendant did not appear and a separation order with 9s per week alimony was granted. WILFUL DAMAGE.—NeIIie Griffin, 5 Garnett's-yard, was summoned by Thomas Cowdell, 31, Legh-street, for damaging property in Dutton-street—lt was stated that defendant broke a window with a brick.—She was ordered to pay the amount of the damage with costs
:VloNDAY.—Before Messrs. F. Moults (in the chair), T. Birchall, J. W. Hayward, S. Wright, H. Thornton, and Alderman Smethurst.

THEFT OF BACON.—George Johnson, a tramp. VMS charged with stealing a side of bacon, of the value of 14s. from a passage near the shop of Joseph Shaw, butcher, Bridge-street.—Prisoner said he was drunk.— The Chief Constable stated that Mr. Tomkinson, Mr. Shaw's assistant, saw the prisoner loitering about ins suspicious manner, and gazing intently into the shop window. He did not see him do anything, however,but shortly after one o'clock, Police-Constable Taylor saw prisoner walking down the street earrying the bacon. Being suspicious that the bacon and the prisoner had not come into each other's company honestly, he ques- tioned the man. Prisoner gave one or two equivocal accounts, but then admitted having stolen it. Mr. Tomkinson came on the scene and identified the bacon As Mr. Shaw's property. Had the prisoner got the bacon to one of the lodging-houses it would have found a ready sale at popular prices.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month.

div.head: Music in the Park.

div.head: Accident to a Warrington Cabman.
div.p: Accident to a Warrington Cabman.

A cabman named Thomas Parker, 44 years of age, who resides at 38, Ashton-street, met with a serious accident on Monday night. He was driving Mr. Dewhurst, J.P. home to Lymm in a hansom early in the evening, and when in the village appeared to become dizzy and fell from the box. He was ren- dered unconscious. The Warrington Horse Ambul- ance was sent for and Parker was conveyed to the Infirmary, where it was found that he had sustained serious injuries to the head. He is progressing favourably.
Personal. Major F. Mac I. Roome returns to the South Lancas- tire Regiment on his completion of five years duty as adjutant of the local volunteer battalion.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
THE ALDERMANIC VACANCY. The Water Engineer and a Coal Contract.

A meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Mr. J.Charlton Parr) presided, and there were also present :—Alderman Fair- clougb, (Deputy Mayor), Aldermen Smethurst, Monks, Sutton, Heaton, Francomb, Bolton, Hutchinson. Coun- cillors Tinnion, Wilkinson, William Roberts, F. R. Roberts, William J. Forshaw, Bennett, Ellison, Baird Rogers, Barton, James Evans, John Evans, Duncan, Davies, Dodds Upson, Lord, Brophy, John Roberts, Peacock, PeAerton, Burton, Craik, with Messrs. Stanley Wilson (deputy Town Clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor). W. S. Haddock (gas engineer), J. Dees (sanitary engineer), A. M. Ker (deputy surveyor).
THE INDISPOSITION OF THE TOWN CLERK,

The MAYOR, at the outset, said they had a very long agenda and some very imi3ortant and intricate business, and he hoped they would go through it very carefully and judiciously with a single eye to the interest of the town and public. He wts sorry to say the Town Clerk was still too unwell t attend. He hoped he would soon get better—(hear, a3ar)—but he was not yet tit to come out.

div.head: NEW ALDERSIAN.
div.p: THE NEW ALDERSIAN.

The MAYOR said the first business was the election of an alderman to fill the place of their much regretted friend, Alderman Shaw Green. The election would lie proceeded with in the usual way. Voting papers weretben distributed, and the MAYOR announced that Councillor Bennett was elected by 18 votes to 13. div.head: ALDERMAN BENNETT REPLIES.
div.p: ALDERMAN BENNETT REPLIES.

Alderman BE*-NErr after making the usual declara- tion, observed that in thanking the Council for the honour which they had done him he should like to ex- press his regret at the circumstances which had ' necessitated an aldermanic vacancy. (Hear, hear.) He had hoped to see Mr. Shaw Green occupying the position of alderman for many years to come, and he thought the Council had lost one of its most distinguished mem- bers, and the town and public one whom it would be almost ,impossible to replace. He regretted that he had been led into competition with Mr. Pierpoint, whose services he should be the last to depreciate. It had been said that some men achieved greatness, some were born to greatness, and some had greatness thrust upon them. He claimed to be in the latter category. He had not sought this honour; he was still young; he had not yet attained aldermanic proportions— (laughter)—and he was quite prepared to wait. He thought the whole term of a man's services ought to be taken into consideration whether interrupted or not, and he would have given way in Mr. Pier- point's favour if the Council would have consented. He had had no alternative but to place himself in the Council's hands. He had voted against the seniority, and he had informed his friends that he didn't want them to vote for him on political grounds or • simply because he was a Conservative. (Hear, hear.) He had always been against the idea of politics in the Council, and he had regretted the attempt to introduce the cloven hoof of oarty politics over his body. He rejoiced exceedingly that in spite of all the beating of party drums the vote had not been made a purely political one, and that he held his new position through the votes of men from whom in politics he very widely differed. In conclusion, he could only thank them warmly for the honour they had done him, and express the hope that he might soon have the privilege of con- gratulating Councillor Pierpoint upon the attainment of a similar position,and promised that he would do his best not,to forget:as an alderman,the confidence which for close upon ten years the electors of the Howley Ward had been good enough to repose in him as a councillor.

div.head: POLICE BUILDINGS.
div.p: THE POLICE BUILDINGS.

On the recommendation of the architects and Borough Surveyor, the Watch Committee decided that the old Armoury adjoining the new police premises be removed, the old materials of which belonged to the contractor; that the inspector's house be com- pleted, and that the proposed additional Inspector's residence be dispensed with; and that on the taking down of the Armoury the wall fronting to Museum- street be completed.
The confirm'ation of the minutes was moved by the MAYOR. The DEPUTY MAYOR seconded.

Councillor LORD said he thought that part referring to the Inspector's house, Scc., should be referred back. A month or two ago they referred this back. Was there any reason why it should be brought forward again? The MAYOR said he was advised that this was work which had to be finished, and that there was a reduction to be made for the old Armoury in the original con- tract which induced the Committee to come to the conclusion that it was best to continue the work.

COW:Will°, PEMBERTON said he thought in rega—rd to the minutes "that the old Armoury adjoining the new police premises be removed, the old material of which belonged to the contractor." . . . that it was hardly fairly stated, because they all knew that in the con- ditions of contracts all these allowances could be adjus- ted between the contractor and the people he was doing the contract for. He thought that as this was put for- ward at the last Council meeting but one, and it went by the vote and was carried by a large majority it should not be gone on with. He could not seeany press- ing necessity for the Armoury, which was a good build- ing, being pulled down at present. Councillor TINNION asked what they were going to do with the site of the old Armoury. They had here simply a statement and no explanation. He could quite see that they could not build or complete the inspector's house without pulling down a portion of the Armoury. He should like to know what was going to be done with the land and what land they would have left after the Armoury and the wall in front of the Armoury was taken down.

The BOROUGH SURVEYOR explained that in the original plans there was a parade room allowed for and two resident inspectors' houses. The Technical Schools had to take possession of the Armoury. The result of that was that the Armoury could not be touched. The parade room could not be completed. The inspectors' houses could not be completed until the Armoury was removed.' As soon as the Technical Schools were re- moved to the new, building the difficulty was removed. The parade room and one only of the resident inventors' houses had to be completed. A portion of the Armoury would be thrown into this inspector's house, the other portion would be thrown into the parade room, and the remainder would be reserved for the land outside. The cost of all this would be considerably less than what it was thought it would be originally. As far as the materials were concerned the contractor allowed a sum of £7OO for them. Of course he had not been able to use the Armoury material. It was only natural he would claim a certain proportion of the amount for loss —not being able to use the old bricks. But that wasinow a matter of arrangement whereby what bricks could be used would betaken by the contractor,the rest would re- main the property of the Corporation and would be sold. Councillor TINNION asked what authority they had to complete the parade room when they only asked for authority to complete the inspector's house. The BOROUGH SURVEYOR said that in the original contract the parade room was included. Councillor TINNION : So were the inspectors' houses. I submit they cannot complete that parade room with- out the sanction of this Council. I think it should be deferred again. _ _
The BOROUGH SURVEYOR stated that at the last meeting instructions were given that amended tenders should be pt._ _ _
CouncillOr PEMBERTON moved that the minutes be passed with the exception of the part relating to the armoury and the inspector's house.
Coxmaillor LORD seconded.

The amendment that the minutes relating to the police buildings be referred back was rejected by 16 votes to 10, the voting being : For the amendment. Against. Councillor James Evans Alderman Fairclough

The minutes of the committee were approved on the motion of Councillor DODDS, seconded by Councillor FoRSHAW.
STREET WIDENING. COST OF MANCHESTER-ROAD IMPROVEMENT.
