voluble member than Mr. Tinnion, and he was a little surprised at the impatience with which he listened to other people. Phis was his (Alderman Bennet.'s)annual opportunity. He intended holding to it, because in spite of the cynicism of certain memaers he knew that all the enlightened opinion of the country was on his side, and he was surprised at Councillor Tinnion being on the side of what was retrogressive to public health ann public pleasure. He did not think the Inspector met with the encouragement that he ought to do in regard to the suppression of the smoke nuisance. a

Alderman BuZioN ob,ected to what he described as the ramoling statements of Alderman Bennett. Alder- man Bennett wanted to inake Warrington one of the blackest towns in England. A certain amount of smoke was to their aivantage. A min ought not to put on coloured spactables and call the town offensive names: and he hoped that when the next annual report came round he should )e,spared this infliction. (Laughter.) Alderman BF.NNETT remarked that he wus borne out by the doctor. • Councillor Lotto said Alderman Bolton lived on the windward side of the town. Councillor PEMBERTON said he thought when War- rington w ts co np trad with other nanufacturing towns in regard to the smoke question, the co nparison was in favour of Warrington. Let them take Sheffield— (laughter)—Widnes, and even Liverpool—let them go down Vauxhall-road and see. If they looked at the tops of chin legs, of course they would sae smoke. RA did not think Alderman Bennett should make such sweeping a isertions. [ls woad find that Warrington compared favourably with other towns. There were more crying evils in Warrington than smoke. (Hear, hear.) "I should," he concluded, "like to see a little more smoke and a little more work." (Hear, hear) Alderman SUTTON said he thought Alderman Bennett was a little out of order in bring this smoke question forward now, because the Health- Co nmittee did not deal with it. They had, however, two or three times called the atteation of the Sanitary Works Committee to the condition of chimneys in Warrington issuing out so much black smoke. He read a letter from Dr. Gordan, in which the writer stated that it was satisfactory to be able to say that from an examination on June 6th he found that the condition of the town's water was ex- cellent.
The minutes were confirmed. SANITARY COIYIKITTER.

The minutes of this co nmittee, which were adopted on the motion of Councillor JOHN EVANS, seconded by Alderman SMETHURST, included the acceptance of the tender of Messrs. J. and P. Round, of Stourbridge, to supply 2,000 galvanized ash cans at ss. 3d. each which were necessary, Councillor Evans said, owing to the difficulty of getting tubs made, and their rapid wear. TOWN HALL, PAR S.S, AND BA.ras COAMITrEE

was accepted subject to the Engineer being satisfied as to the quality. The shortest and most correct answer he could give to the first question was that he did not know. (Laughter.) He knew nothing about the ques- tions, and he did not know but what Messrs. Evans were actually supplying the slack and coal until he saw the questions on the agenda. Neither did he think a single member of his committee knew a word about it. He had seen Mr. Dais and had gone carefully into the matter with him. He (Alderman Francomb) did not wish to give the Council all that had been given to him, because he thought it would cast reflections on people he would not like to see in any way held up to ridicule. Bat this was Mr. Deas'sjexplanition as far as he could give it. The first meeting of the committee after the sample had been tested was on May 25th, but owing to pressure of business he (Mr. Deas) regretted the matter hid escaped his memory. At the next meeting, on June Bth, he was unfortunately absent, and the matter was not brought forward as he intended to make a personal' explanation. The explanation concluded: "On the whole , I am confident that the interests of the Corporation have lin no way suffered." The answer to question No 2 was 100 tons a month, but it seemed they used con- siderably more. In answer to question No 3, 41 tons 9 cwt. was supplied in April; 3 tons 10 cwt. in May ; and in June so far none at all. In answer to question No. 4, the contractors were supplying none at the present time. Inanswer to question No. 5, at the present time and clarity, the whole of the time men- tioned, supplies were being sent in by the Warrington Slate Company, and in regard to question No. 6, only one firm had supplied namely, the Slate Company, and the quantities were : April, 153 tons 7 cwts., May, 149 tons 1 cwt. 1 qr. • and June, 80 tons. He must say that he had been to the books of the Water Co nmittee, and he could find nothing out about asking anyone's stuff to be tested; but he believed the members of the -Com- mittee would bear him out when he said that it was decided that the slack should be tested; and, he believed, there was some discretionary power given to Mr. Deas that if it did not turn out ri*ht somebody else's should be purchased. But that question Was never brought before the Committee, which was certainly a mistake. (Hear, hear.) While he had given them the exact reason why the Committee did not know anything about it, and though somebody else's stuff seemed to have given greater satisfaction, he did think the ques- tion of changing ought to have been brought before the Committee. They could not have any discussion on the report at that meeting. He would be only too glad if they could.
Alderman FRANCOMB: Is there any question you would like to ask?

Councillor LORD: No more, thank you. (Laughter.) Councillor PEMBERTON said he would like to make a personal explanation with regard to Messrs. Evans and Co.. but he was ruled out of order by the Mayor, who pointed out that the water committee's minutes were not yet before the Council. Alderman FRANCOMB then moved tbe adoption of the minutes of the water Committee, which stated that Councillor Duncan had been appointed a member of the committee and it was decided that the new reservoir and works executed under the powers of the 1899 Act be formally opened on June 30th. He said the amount spent on the works up to the present time was £135,000, and the committee would like the Council to see how the money had been expended. They were drawing from that source 600,000 gallons per day and if they required it they expected to be able to supply 1,250,000 gallons extra per day. Councillor JOHN EVANS seconded. Councillor PEMBERTON moved that the whole of the minutes be referred back, after the explanation Alder- man Fr tncomb had given them. The explanation only showed how difficult it was for every member of the Council Co carry out his duties. As a member of the Water Committee he knew nothing about this affair. Fancy this going on for three months, and an official never to report one word about it! It only showed them the possibilities of what could go on in that Corporation, and as a protest against the whole transaction he moved that the minutes be referred back.

Councillor CRNIK seconded the proposition of Coun- cillor Pemberton, after the very unbusinesslike state- ment made by Alderman Francomb in regard to the purchase of slack. He thought if the Alderman could not give a better explanation of a small purchase of that description he was a very poor one to give an explana- tion of the expenditure of £135,000 upon waterworks. Alderman Francomb seemed to know nothing whatever about the work of the Water Committee. He had left it to his benchman Mr. Deas, and Mr. Was seemed to have left it to somebody else, and he knew nothing about it. (Laughter.) In the circumstances, he thought they would be quite justified in referring these minutes back.

Councillor JAMES EVANS said he supposed each com- mittee had the option of rejecting any contract entered into if the material supplied was not equal to the sample. (Hear, hear.) He wished to know if the committee, instead of leaving the matter in the hands of an official ought not to have entered into a second contract. If Alderman Francomb had been prepared to make a state- men that the Slate Company's. tender was the second lowest he took it that the Chairman and officials of the committee would be justified in selecting that tender. He thought it remiss that another firm should be supply- ing what was originally tendered for without a second tender having been asked for. Alderman FRANCOMB: I don't think this sort of in- sinuation should be thrown out.
Councillor JAMES EVANS ian not in.sinuating any- thing. They are facts.

Arderman-PaANcome: I don't mean to say you are wilfully telling fibs, but you are stating what is absolutely untrue. The fact of the matter was that this tender was received and accepted by the Water Committee as the lowest tender on April 7th. I have purposely kept Richard Evans and Company's name out of the matter simply because there are statements in the report which I think are actually unfair to them. The Slate Company's was the next lowest tender. It was decided to try this slack and as the committee never heard a word about it we naturally supposed that Richard Evans and Company had got the contract, and how in the world am I to know whether Mr. Dens has got RichardEvans's slack or somebody else's until I am shown it in this way? (pointing to Councillor Lord's questions). I naturally supposed—and so did every member of the committee—Richard Evans and Com- pany ware supplying the slack, and if Mr. Dens had done what he ought to have done he would have come to the committee and said: "This does not suit me, the Slate Company's suit better "—(a Voice: "Exactly ") and we should then have entered into a contract with the Slate Company. Until I saw it on this paper I had not the slightest idea that Richard Evans and Company were not supplying the slack. I think it is very unfair for Councillor Craik to make use of such expressions as "the unbusine,sslike statement of Alderman Francomb." Where is the unbusinesslike statement? Do you blame me for all the official's neglect? Councillor CIL.IIK : T blame you for not knowing more about it.
Alderman FRANCO= : We have been buying slack for the last ten or twelve years in this way. We have never had a case like this before.
Councillor PEMBERTON : Yes. Alderman FRA.NCOMB I know nothing of it. (Laughter.) Councillor JAMES EVANS (to Alderman Francomb): It is a bold statement for you to say I was absolutely 1 yin.g..

Alderman FaANcomn : I said you were insinuating. Councillor JAMES EVANS : You said I was lying. The MAYOR said he did not understand Alderman Francomb's remark in the sense or he should have checked it. (Hear, hear.) Alderman FRANCOMB : I withdraw, of course, if I said that.

Councillor JAMES EVANS : I only stated to the Council what Alderman Francomb has broadly admitted to be true and neither intentionally nor unintentionally was I misrepresenting the truth(to Alderman Francomb) I dont say you are in full knowledge of the facts, I dont put the onus of the position upon you as chairman of the committee; what I say, sir, is that after your admission you should have known— Alderman FRANCOMB : How could I tell? Councillor JAMES EVANS : Wait a moment. How can you tell? Surely when an official of the Corpora- tion has taken upon himself not to acquaint the Chair- man of a Committee with an important matter such as this, that which we are just now considering with regard to slack—surely the chairman should be better posted up in the position. (Hear, hear.) Alderman FRANCOMB: Ido not think yon under- stand it now.
Councillor JAMES EvANS : Ido understand it. Aldermen FRANCOME : Can I rise to a point for order?

Councillor EVANS: I think not; I think lam in p ossossion. The MAYOR (to Alderman Francomb) : Take a note of the point and deal with it in your reply. Councillor JAMES EVANS : To say the least of this matter is to say this : That the buying of this slack is in a very loose and unbusinesslike condition. Alderman FRANCOMB : Not so far as the committee is concerned.
Councillor JAMES EVANS : I take it that the Water Committee are disposed to throw the onus of this upon the official?
Alderman FR,INCOMB: What else could you do ? You have the official's words.

Councillor EVANS: If you left the official at liberty to please himself whether he took the second lowest contract or not—which I think would have been ft proper thing to do—l am not complaining otthe War- rington Slate Company's contract, but I do say that no official has any right to undertake such a step as this without acquainting the committee. Councillor JOHN EVANS: So we all say. Councillor JAMES EVANS: So you all say? Councillor JOHN EVANS: Yes.

Councillor JAMBS EVANS : I am going to content myself with saying this: That the Water Committee should be better up, and know more about its own busi- ness than is evident from the statement of Alderman Francomb. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BOLTON said there appeared to have been a little irregularity about this transa.ction, but he thought the best course to adopt would be to ask the committee to consider the matter, and obtain a proper explanation. He had not the slightest doubt that they would be quite capable of doing their own business and be quite strong enough to rectify the irregularity. (Hear, hear.) There was no firm in existence that did not have

art occasional mistake made by its officials. He thought the irregularity had only been a slip and he did not think Corporation had suffered. He did not think there had been any fraud or anything of that description. It had simply been an accident. He was of the opinion that if the Water Committee was left to deal with the matter the result would be quite satisfactory. Referring the minutes back would do no good. If they were going to pass a vote of cen- sure on the committee let them pass it. (Hear, heat, and laughter.) Councillor DODDS thought Alderman Francomb's statement an honest and straightforward explanation of the case as it stood. (Hear, hear.) He suggested that the mover of the amendment, having brought out the facts, might let the amendment go. (Hear, hear.) Councillor TINNCON said he thought the matter was most important, and he thought the whole circum- stances should be gone into by the Committee, who should have instructions to report to the next Council meeting • but he did say that while throwing the blame on the official the committee were to blame. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Francomb said he knew nothing about it; his reply was that he ought to have known some- thing about it. (Hear, hear.) During Aprills9 tons of slack was supplied by the Warrington Slate Company. When were those 159 tons paid for, and when was the account passed ? The MA.YOR called Councillor Tinnion to order, as he was going outside the minutes and back again to Coun- cillor Lord's questions. Councillor latsxtox asked whether payments for slack were not included in the minutes under discussion. The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK: Yes. Councillor Tmrox: Then lam in order in discuss- ing the accounts of the committee. (Hear, hear.) Continuing, he said at any rate the whole of the com- mittee, or a portion of it, had passed accounts for the paktnent for 159 tons of slack supplied by the Warring- ton Slote Company, and they should have known their contract was with Richard Evans and Company, and should have asked themselves how it was they were passing accounts for the Warrington Slate Company, aid not with Richard _Evans and Company. (Hear, hear.) It was all yeery well to blame the official. The official had admitted his fault, and he thought itt would be more manly if the committee admitted their fault. There had been some remissness, but it had been all round, and the whole blame did not rest with the officials. He thought the best course to adopt would be to leave the whole matter inabeyance till the committee were prepared to report fully to the Council. Alderman MONKS said he thought some members overlooked the fact that a certain amount of discretion was left to the engineer. It must of necessity take time to test the slack, and it did not seeman unreason- able amount of time to spend over making this test. Alderman SUWON said that while every member was justified in calling attention to irregularities, he thought it only fair and reasonable to listen to explanations; but there seetneda disposition on the part of some members to persist in making trouble and inpreventing business from going on in a smooth—(hear, hear.)— straightforward and proper manner, (Hear, hear.) They often discarded the lowest tender because they found the next one preferable. He believed the official in this case did his best for the Corporation, and that everything he did was in the interests of the Corporation and so long as that explanation was given he did notsee that there was any reason to go further into the matter Although they were aware that perhaps the transaction had been made in the interests of the Council certain members seemed disposed to introduc bother and trouble on the subject. Councillor W. ROBERTS said it was only fairto the official to say this: He (the speaker) was in the room waiting for another committee meeting when he heard it distinctly stated to Mr. Deas that if the sample or supply was not satisfactory he was to take the next lowest tender.

The MAYOR suggested that the amendment might be withdrawn on the understanding that the committee would ininire and report. Councillor LORD thought the question ought to be gone into as he ha l heard from others who had been treated similarly.

The MAYOR said he understood the matter would be considered by the committee and reported upon. Alderman FRANCOMB, in reply, regretted that Messrs. Evans' name had been forced into the discussion. He did not want to say anything that would interfere with the firm because he thought they had been rather roughly treated. (Hear, hear.) He was fully of the opinion that none of the members of the committee knew that Messrs. Evans were not actually supplying the slack. Mr. Deas told him that he had had considerable trouble in the past and the only mistake he had made was in not mentioning the matter to the committee. He (the speaker) was exeeedingly sorry that the irregularity had occurred. - On beingput to the vote only Councillors Craik and Pemberton voted for the amendment. The MA.Yon : I think I need not trouble the other gentlemen to stand up. The minutes were then carried.

--- GRATUMES TO TRAMWAY' ENIPLOYEEs. I The Electricity and Tramways Committee recom- mended that gratuities be given to the following employees for exemplary conduct since their appoint- ment:—James Ellis 10s., W. Warburton 7s. 6d., H. Warburton 75. 6d. Mr. Alderman MONKS in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said the gratuities were intended as a sort of reward in appreciation of their services. The first name on the list was a driver who had driven without a single accident. The gratuities were to encourage drivers to take extreme care in their work. Alderman SUTTON seconded and the minutes were agreed to.

div.head: PAD G ATE-LANE.
div.p: PAD G ATE-LANE.

For the purpose of carrying out the widening of Padgate-lane, the committee also resalved.—" That the Corporation agree to purchase from Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company, Limited, the plot of land be- longing to the company containing 1,950 square yards at 3d. per square yard and 25 years purchase, tint so much of the land as is required for the widening of the road, viz, 388 yards, be retained, and that the remainder of the land be given in eKchange to Colonel Ireland Blackburne for other land required from him for the further widening of the road. The difference in value to be paid by Colonel Bla.ckburne."

I. W !KWIC K-STREET. It was further decided that £5O be paid to Messrs. Greenall, Wnitley and Co., Limited, for a strip of land in front of the King's Head Inn, Winwick-street required for the widening of that street.

div.head: ARPLEY-ROAD.
div.p: ARPLEY-ROAD.

The qmstion of the proposed improvement at the corner of Arpley-road and Wilson-Patten-street was considered at a meeting of the Committee, and it was resolved that no further steps be taken with regard to it.

div.head: LIVI3RPOOL-ROAD.
div.p: LIVI3RPOOL-ROAD.

The committee received a letter from Messrs. Joseph Oros&ld and Sons, Ltd., with reference to the pre- scribed line through part of their premises in Liverpool- road, and suggesting that as they require to make alterations to their works forthwith it should be referred to some one valuer to settle all questions affecting that company, Greenall, Whitley and Co., Ltd., and the Corporation.

div.head: BUILDING INSPECTOR.
div.p: THE BUILDING INSPECTOR.

The committee also recommended tliE4 Mr. W. Sugars, of Scarborough, be appointed Building Inspector at a salary of £lOO per annum, rising by annual increments of £5 to a maximum of £l2O. PROPOSED NEW STREET. SOIKEY-STR.EET TO FRIARS'-GATE. -

The Street Improvement Committee- submitted and recommended for approval a proposal for making a new street to run from Sankey-street on the west side of Trinity Church to Rylands-street and Friars'-gate, .via the Eagle and Child yard. The plan of the street as far as the Eagle and Child yard was submitted to the committee by Mr. R. E. Garnett, who proposes to give a plot of land contlining 691 square yards extending from the rear of Mr. Benson's premises to the Eagle and Child yard in exchange for a plot of land contain- ing 920 square yards purchased by the Corporation from the late Mr. Thomas Hewitt. Mr. Garnett will also give to the Corporation two plots of land, containing 181 square yards and 47 square yards respectively, and consent to the buildings standing thereon being taken down on payment to him of £B5O towards the cost of erecting similar buildings. The Corporation will retain a strip of land 15ft. wide, containing 247 square yards, part of the site of the passage proposed to be con- structed by the Corporation. The Corporation will seek powers to purchase the necessary land for the continua- tion;of the new street from the Eagle and Child yard to Rylands-street. Messrs. Hodgkinson,Limited, agree to give up 47 square yards of land for an equal area of land now forming part of the Eagle and Child yard, and Mr. T. B. Carter agrees to the proposed work on condition that his claims for compensation are not prejudiced. The Corporation will make and pave the street. Alderman SuTroN moved the adoption of the minutes with the exception of those relating to the proposed new street from Sankey-street to Rylands-street, as some members of the Committee and Council thought it advisable that the question should be referred back for re-consideration. (Hear, hear.) Councillor WILKINSON seconded the motion.

Councillor PEMBERTON, referring to the ia-dgate-lane widening, said he thought the 25 years' purchase for unsecured ground rent was excessive and quite out of the market value. The man in the street knew it was ridiculous. He thought 22 years would be ample. In regard to the application of Messrs. Crosfield, he did not think it fair to leave it to one man to settle the price. Alderman Surros said he disagreed with Councillor Pemberton in reference to the price they paid for land from Messrs. Greenall. Whitley and Co. He (Alderman Sutton) thought, and he believed the Committee thought, they were very successful and lucky in getting the land at the price. They had paid higher prices in Warrington for land required for similar purposes. They had paid 4d. a yard for 25 years' purchase for land in Manchester-road. People were not disposed to part with land at that price. It was difficult to purchase land at all, and he thought they were buying land atl"a very reasonable price indeed. Councillor TINNION : What is Colonel Blackburne going to pay you?

Alaerm'an-StITTos : The same price. We give and take, and I know you cannot co and purchase land from either Colonel Blackburne or any other landowner at the sane price Councillor TINNION : Is he paying 3d. to us for the difference? Alderman SuTToN: Yes.

Councillor CRALK asked- where was the land that Colonel Blackburne was to be paid £BB2 for.He thought that the Council ought to be put in possession of the particulars of the purchase. Alderman SUTTON said the Councillors could have the particulars if they would go to the trouble to ask for them before they came to the meetings. Hew was it possible to keep everything mono's mind? He wished the members would go into the matter before-hand. With regard to Messrs. Crosfield, they had full confi- dence in the valuer doing what was right as between the Corporation and that firm, both of whom were desirous of doing what was fair and right. Councillor PEMBERTON claimed to move an amend- ment.

The DEPUTY Tows CLERK, however, ruled that no further speeches could be made on the minutes, Alder- man Sutton having replied. The minutes were then adotped, with the exception of those relating to the proposed new street.

div.head: HEALTH COAMIT TEE.
div.p: HEALTH COAMIT TEE.

This committee have app3lnted their Chairman Deputy-Chairman and the Medical 0 llcer of Health to attend the annual Congress of the Sanitary Institute, at Bradford, from July 7th to July 11th. Alderman' Smethurst, Councillors Jas. Evans, Wilkinson and Barton were appointed a sub-committee to consider tenders for fire-escapes, Scc., at the Sanatorium at Sankey, while the Medical o.ficar of Health was appointed the registrar for the purposes of the Mid- wives Act, 1902, with his office as the registration onlice under that Act. The Medical 0 ficer of Health reported that Inspector Nightingale had heen appointed Chief Inspector of Nuisances under ther Bromley Rural Dis- trict Council. Resolved,—that he advertise for a successor:

Alderman SUTTON proposed the minutes of the Health Committee; and Alderman Smethurst seconded. Alderman BENNEFT referred to the Medical Officer's report, a summary of which was published in last Saturday's "Examiner." He found, he said, that he was amply repaid for the time taken in studying it. He should like to call attention to the matter of the water supply. There must have been some serious remissness on the part of the water department in not acquainting the doctor when No 1 shaft was used, because there was contamin- ation which might have been dangerous to the public health. Another point be had to refer to was that hardly annual, the smoke nuisance. He contended that the doctor's observations thereon were a sweeping con- demnation that was thoroughly deserved. Dr. Gornall used strong language but not a whit too strong. Every syllable of it was absolutely true. The Inspeetor, in his report, tried to minimise matters and infered that they were doing pretty well, but he,(Alderman Bennett) did not think they were doing well at all if there was only one complaint made during the year in atmosphere as poisonous as was that of Warrington from day to day. Alderman BOLTON.—Question, question. Alderman BENNETT.—WeII, let me finish and then question as you like. Alderman BOLTON: Don't any" poisonous." Alderman BENNETT: Well, it is extremely unsatis- factory if there has only been one complaint. They were told two hundred and twenty-four observations had been made. Where had they been made? There had been six notices served mid one fine inflict'ed. He thought this was the reductio and absurdum, because if their Inspector kept his eyes open there would be more notices served and more fines inflicted. He was constantly seeing chimneys violating the Act. Councillor DAVIES said the Corporation was one of the worse offenders. Alderman BENNETT observed that it seemed to him remarkable that in connection with the electricity de- partment there shomld be so much smoke. He con- sidered thatthis smoke nuisance was greater that it was seven or eight years ago when he came to live in the town. Judging by the criterion of his own garden it was difficult to get vegetation to flourish. Councillor TIN. NION : You are a bad gardener. (Laughter.) _ _ _ _ - -

, Alderman BENNETT said he did not look after the garden himself. He had a very experienced gardener, and all his efforts were unavailing. (Councillor TINNION : "Time time.") There was really not amok+

div.head: COMPLAINT ABOUr THE PRIVATE BA.TFIS.
div.p: A COMPLAINT ABOUr THE PRIVATE BA.TFIS.

At a me3ting of this committee, it was resolved that a framed artist proof etching of the recent picture of 11. M. &hag Eds trd punted by Mr. Luke Fildes R.A., bepurchased at a cost of £l5 15s. ; that the best &tanks of the committee be given to Mr. John Henderson, of Hinchley Wood, Ashbourne, for his gift to the avairy of a silver cock phe tsant; that the staff and employees of the Electricity and Tramways Dap trtment be allowed the use of the baths at the r3ducel charges made to other employees of the Corporation, viz.:—.ss. for a season ticket, or 2d. for single admission. Alderman 304T0N pr tposei the •adoption of the minutes and said it was proposed to purchase the picture to ornament the fire place in the hall. Alderman SALE rfluasr seconded.

Councillor PINNIoN said he had received complaints from parsons using the private baths. The hot and cold water taps were turned on and afterwards the attenuant went away with tha key and considered that he was the fit and proper person to say what the temperature of the bath should be. It got up to almest 90 degrees sometimes, and the man had to take the bath or leave it. Many gentlemen had co uplained of having caught cold as the result. S01:113 provision might be made to regulate the temperature. Alder nan BENNETT asked what facilities were granted to school children in the %viva reduced charges. Councillor PEMBERTON said he had always found the attendants most civil and obliging and he understood they were asting upon official instructions in taking away the keyafter turning on the water. The proper remedy would be to provide keys for all the baths. Alderman BOLTON said Coancillor Tinnion had pre- viously drawn his attention to the matter and the committee ordered it to be remedied as much as pos- sible. It was a rather dmgerous matter to leave the key with a bather because he might scald himself or do some other mischief. The turning on of the taps must be in the hands of some responsible person as they did not want anyone to be boiled or frozen. fhe committee had ordered the attendants to obtain thermometers and test the water each time it was necessary. School children were admitted at a charge of one penny each under the supervision of a teacher on certain days. The committee were doing everything they could for the convenience of the public by supplying them with more accommodation than could be obtaine I elsewhere. The nrinutes were confirmed. THE BIG GAS PROFITS. ALDERMAN FAIRCLOUGH'S INTERESTING STATEMENT.

At a meeting of the Gas Committee it was resolved that the price of gas for lighting purposes be reduced from 2s. 7d. to 2s. 61. net per 1,000 cubic feet. The question of reducing the price of gas for power purposes is to be considered at a meeting of the committee on the 26th inst. The Gas En.zineer was authorized to purchase 500 slot cookers for letting out on hire. Alderman FAIRdLOUGH, in proposing the adoption of the minutes, said: It will be of interest to the mem- bers of the Council to hear th it we have had a vary successful year at the Gas Works, the gross profit for the year ending 31st March last being £16,522, which is the largest made since the purchase of the gas works, It. is £6,000 more than the average of the previous five years. After deducting the charges for sinking fund and interest it will leave .28,381. to be transferred in relief of rates in accordance with the Act of Parliament. I may re:nark here that this trans- fer of .8,381 to the relief of rates will make a total of £20,090 contributed since they have been in our possession. £8,075 has also been placed in a reserve fund which with accumulations of interesE now amounts to £10,031 Tnere has also been a reduc- tion in street lighting of its. per lamp, and there are 1,511 lamps affected. The proposed reduction of id. in the price of gas will make a total redaction of is. per thousand oabic feet since the works came into our possession. This id. reduction will absorb about £1,150 of the profit. The eJnamittee do not think it advisable to make any reduction beyond the Id. at present, as we have to consider the possibility of the profits not being so large next year, the profits depending largely upon the price of coal to be bought and the price of i residuals to be sold. There s also at the pre- sent time a large expenditure to meet for education purposes and street improvements. In the extension of 1896 differential rating was granted to several areas brought into the borough. In a few years these districts will be on the full rating which will produce a sum equal to 2d. in the 2.1 f the profit next year should be as large as this year's, the committee will no doubt consider the desirability of making a further reduction in the price of gas, but in dealing with the provision of profits it should not be overlooked that the ratepayers who are responsible for the debt on the undertaking should have the first consideration, as in case there should be a loss they alone would have to meet it. Alderman BOLTON seconded.

The MAYOR said they might all congratulate the Chairman corn nittee, and the town generally on the very satisfactory report they had heard. (Hear' hear.) Councillor DODDS joined in the congratulations but remarked that the quality of the gas at Penketl was very poor at times. On Saturday he could not get enough light to read from four incandescent lights. Mr. HADDOCK, gas engineer, said he could not explain the reason at present, but would inquire into the matter.

- Alderman FRANCOMB said he was in a similar position to Councillor Dodds on two occasions last week but after the matter was mentioned to an official of the gas department the supply was improved and he had had a beautiful light ever since. The minutes were approved. KNUTSFORD-ROAD WIDENING.

The Rivers Committee resolved that the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee be requested to consider the advisability of widening Knutsford-road and constructing a permanent rubble wall. On the motion of Aldorman BOLTON, seconded by Alderman HUTCHINSON, the minutes of the committee were passed. THE 'FIRE BRIGADE. INCREASE OF SALARIES.

The Fire Engine Committee decided that the salary of the superintendent be increased from £3O to £45 per annum, and the salary of the deputy-superintendent from £7 15s to £l3 per annum. The minutes were confirmed on the proposition of Alderman SMETEIURST who explained that Super- indendent Turner had been in the brigade about forty years and had not received an advance for the past ten years. His son had served for ten years and this was his first advance. COUNCILLOR LORD AND A WATER COM- MITTEE CONTRACT, SINGULAR PROCEDURE. THE COMMITTEE IN IGNORANCE.

• COUriCillOe LORD asked the Chairman of the Water Committee the following questions with regard to the resolution passed by the Council, on April 7th: "That the tender of Messrs. R. Evans and Company, Limited, to supply washed slack and coal for six months, accord- ing to schedule of prices, be accepted, subject to the engineer being ,satisfied as to the quality ":—(l) Why has not this resolution been carried out? (2) What is the average.monthly consumption of slack as required per the contract in question? (3) What quantity was supplied by the contractor in April, May, and June, to date? (4) Are the contractors supplying all the slack and coal as per contract? (5) If not, what firm or firms ttre sending in supplies? (6) What quantities have been supplied during the said periods (under the specific contract) by firms other than the accepted oon- tractor, and what .quantity has each firm supplied? div.head: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
div.p: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
A PROTEST BY MESSRS. PAIRCLOUGI-1 AND SONS.

The following letter of protest from Messrs. James Fairclough and Sons was read at. a meeting of the general Purposes Committee :—" Mersey Mills, War- rington, May 16th, 1903. Dear sir,—We notice that the Corporation are carrying a line of pipes across the river alongside of Warrington Bridge, supported on brackets from the bridge. The navigation under the bridge is extremely difficult even under present conditions, and anything which has the effect of widening the bridge adds more seriously to this difficulty. We have no de- sire to hamper the Corporation in any way, but we must protest against anything which will render the passage of our vessels more dangerous or difficult." COUNCILLOR BARTON'S APPOINTMENT ON THE PARLIAMENTARY SUB-COMMITTEE. AN AMENDMENT BY COUNCILLOR WILLIAM ROBERTS.

It was resolved that Alderman Sutton be re-elected a representative governor of the Warrington Grammar School .—Councillo r Barton and Councillor Ellison were appointed members of the Parliamentary Sub-Commit- tee and Parr Hall Sub-Committee respectively. On the recommendation of the Parr Hall Committee the tender of Hesketh and Son, Limited, for the painting and decorating of the Parr Hall according to specification at £360 was accepted. The MAYOR moved and Alderman SUTTON seconded the adoption of the minutes.

Councillor WITLum ROBERTS moved an amendment that the name of Councillor Forshaw be substituted for Councillor Barton on the Parliamentary Sub-Committee, on the ground that the resolution was passed when there were eight members of the Council detained in an adjoining room. He had not one word to say against Councillor Barton as an individual but he thought there were gentlemen in that Council who had served much longer and were more entitled to consideration for that important position. He thought a gentleman with a legal training would be more suitable for the position and he therefore proposed that Councillor Forshaw's name be substituted.
Alderman SUTTON said it had been the custom to select members who had had the largest experience in municipal matters.
Councillor TINNEON : You ought to have elected me then: (Laughter.) _

_ Alderman SUTTON: Perhaps your turn may come some day. Continuing, he said Councillor Barton had always done his best, but legal knowledge was some- times required, had it would be in the interests of the town and the Council to have a member with knowledge and experience of law. He seconded the amendment. The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK ruled that the matter was not in order. They could confirm or otherwise the minutes, but to aulistitute a name would have to come forward in the proper way. _

Councillor Wm: ROBERTS then moved that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of the minute relating to Councillor Barton. Councillor DODDS hoped the amendment would not be pressed. He thought the matter might be allowed to go on for twelve months. He believed Mr. Barton was well qualified for the position. The argument used by Councillor William Roberts might apply to himself, because he had had no municipal experience whatever. Mr. Barton had had some months experience. On per- sonal grounds it would be an unkind cut to put him off and he hoped the amendment would not be persisted in.

Councillor PF,MBERTON did not think the present was an opportune time to give any member of the Council , such an unkind cut as was proposed. Those gentlemen who wanted to bring candidates forward should attend the meeting. Alderman HUTCHINSON said the Markets Committee was meeting at the time and the members were unable to attend the meeting of the General Purposes Com- mittee.
Alderman BOLTON did not 'think that the Parliamen- tarysub-Committee would meet before next November. (Laughter.) It was very seldom that the committee waS called together.
Councillor -TINstoN said he was not present at the meeting of the General Purposes Committee but he thought it was unfair to bring this matter forward now that the appointment had been made._ _ _
CotmcillOr Wi-LLIAm ROBERTS said he brought this forward as a protest. He had noticed during the past twelve months one or two tricks of that kind.

Councillor JAMES EVANS said he was the mover of the resolution, and he would have no trickery attached to him. (Laughter). Councillor WILLIAM ROBERTS said he withdrew the remark as soon as he made it. What he meant to say was that several new members had been placed on com- mittees during the last twelve months over theheads of members who had been connected with the Council for

div.p: More Judgment than Luck.
A lady writes: "I haVe brought up fiVe children, youngest now nine, and haVe neVer had one case of Measles amongst them. I have never used any soap IN THE NURSERY except
Wright's Coal Tar Soap.
It must be the Soap, and not pure luck." FOUR-PENCE per Tablet.

THE REPRESENTATION QUESTION. The Clerk reported the receipt of a letter from Mr. Potts, clerk to the County Council, acknowledging the receipt of a resolution asking for the number of Parish Councillors to be increased from seven to twelve. The matter would have the attention of the Council. A DANGEROUS CORNER. The Chairman said he would like to draw the atten- tion of the Council to the dangerous corner at the south-east of Victoria-square. He had seen motorists and cyclists passing the corner at a rapid pace, and whenever he saw them he felt there was danger of collision : the drivers of vehicles being unable to see ahead. He moved that the attention of the County Council be called to the matter,and that they be reques- ted to make some improvement as soon as possible. THE EDUCATIONAL NEEDS OF THE DISTRICT. The Clerk read a requisition which had been for- warded to the Chairman asking that a parish meeting should be called at as early a date as possible' to con- sider the need of erecting a new school in the district. The following signatures were appended :—E. England, E. Lloyd-Jones, W. H. Sherburn, A. H. Dunn, J. Miller, J. Poulson, K. Summerfield, F. Acton, E. Miller, W. Arnold, E. J. Spencer, J. Moss, jemr„ Rev. J. S. Hughes, Wm. Ford, S. Albin.son, and J. Shenton. The Chairman said the requisition was perfectly in order and they had no option but to fix a date. The matter did not rest with the Parish Council but purely with the ratepayers who desired the meeting. There was no doubt that additional school accommodation was needed and the County Council official who had recently inspected the existing school said the accommodation was greatly inadequate. It was decided to hold a parish meeting on Tuesday. the 23rd inst.
SAVING A MAN WITH A DISLOCATED NECK.

Efforts are being made by the physicians of a well- known hospital to save the life of a man named Her- bert, 31 years old, whose neck was dislocated by a blow on the head from a heavy bar -of steel. When Herbert was admitted to the hospital he was wholly paralysed. As a last resort the doctors performed the operation of "extension and counter extension" by slipping a leather collar round the patient's neck and pulling on neck and feet until the dislocated parts of the spinal column slipped back into place.

Martin and Mr. W.Pollitt represented the Ormskirk-street Congregational Church, and an.ong others present were Dr. Casey, Mr. William Smith, Mr. J. Gilchrist, Mr. A. Kay, Mr. E. W. Swift, Mr. J. G. Walton, and others. In the church the service was conducted by the Rev. A. Kirk, the Rev. John Yonge giving the address. The Rev. John Yonge, in paying a tribute to the memory of the deceased minister, said Mr. Parry began his work as his colleague at Warrington. He came direct from Lancashire College where he had secured the love and cordial respect of his tutors and students. He came to Warrington in 1884. an 4 threw himself earnestly into the work of the mission to which he was attached. He often worked beyond the limits of his physical powers, foi, he was never very robust, but he loved his work and rejoiced in being of service. Their people at Warrington parted with him with sincere regard and universal esteem when he was called to minister at Peasley Cross in 1888. He ministered thereuntil 1901, when he found it necessary to relinquish work. He was a faithful, earnest,reliable, useful servant of his Master, and the many generous kindnesses shown him by the people there, and other friends during his illness were testimonies of the res- pect and confidence in which he was held. The best tribute they could give to his memory was to say that he was a good minister of Jesus Christ. To the best of his ability, to the full of his opportunity, to the truest of his knowledge and understanding he ever strove to ,be faithful. He made no pretensions, and sought no prominence, but he strove to be faithful. He was a preacher, a pastor, a teacher, and a friend, and though dead his life still spoke to them. At the grave side the Rev. John Yoqge conducted the burial service, assisted by the Rev, J, Peron Jones. The coffin was covered with floral tributes.

div.head: SLAVERY STILL TEIRI 'TING.
div.p: SLAVERY STILL TEIRI 'TING.

The Rev. W. M. Morrison, an American missionary who has spent the last six and a half years the Congo Free State, returned recently and said : " Slavery practically exists in the Congo. Humanitarianism mid commercialism are at odds there. Concessions or grants of land, however small, can now no longer be obtained from the state by other than favoured industrial cor- porations. Not only are concessions refused to traders, but they are refused also to missionaries. Natives are obliged to work for the government without 'fay. Some who have refused to work in the indiarubber district, in which King Leopold of Belgium practically has abso- lute control, have had their hands cut off. Women are sold into slavery. div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT FOOTBALL ASSOCIATION. Annual Meeting.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT FOOTBALL ASSOCIATION. Annual Meeting.
The annual general meeting of this association was held at the Patten Arms Hotel on Thursday last week. Mr. J. Harvey presided over a fair attendance of representatives.

div.head: REPORT.
div.p: THE REPORT.

The SECRETARY (Mr. T. B. Bradshaw) presented his fifth annual report and statement of accounts, which showed that the cup competition for the past season was a great success, the final tie between Thelwall and Oughtrington producing a record gate for Association football in the district. The gate receipts amounted to £4O 18s., and the expenditure +l2 is. 9d., leaving a balance of £2B 6s, 3d. He regretted that misconduct on the part of players and spectators was on the increase, 50 players and three clubs having been reported and dealt with during the season. One ground was closed and two clubs were ordered to have bills printed and posted on the ground and dressing-room,warning specta- tors as to future conduct. They were now in a fair condition financially, and they had met all their liabili- ties, paid off the overdraft at the bank, and the start next season would be made with a clean record. In addition to the balance carried forward, the President had promised a donation of five guineas. The CHAIRMAN moved the adoption of the report, which was seconded by Sergeant Wilson, and carried unanimously.

div.head: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.
div.p: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

The Rev. F. CLIFTON SMITH was re-elected president. The vice-presidents, with the addition of the name of Mr. J. Fulton Smith, were also elected. The Chairman (Mr. J. Harvey), the secretary (Mr. T. P. Bradshaw), and the treasurer (Mr. Hind), were also re-elected. The five members for the Warrington division on the executive were selected as follows :—Messrs. W. H. Smalley, T. B. Fortes, A. J. Titmas, Sergeant Wilson, and Quartermaster-sergeant Hollins. Mr. Percy Booth was elected on the executive as representative for Dares- bury and Moore Football Club. The election of repre- sentatives for St. Helens, Widnes, and another for Cheshire was left to the Executive Committee. Messrs. Forbes and Smalley were re-elected auditors. Alteration of rules relating to the cup ties were made, and the meeting terminated with votes of thanks to the officers and the press.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR. 1 OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Baptist Church Golborne-street.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR. 1 OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. Baptist Church Golborne-street.
N dricE TO CORRESPONDENTS:
Authors of letters intended for publication must mall cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith.

Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible,not later than Thursday. Correspondents are strongly advised to write briefly. A short letter has a much greater chance of insertion than a long one. We cannot under ordinary cir cumstancesundertake return themanuscripts which are not used.

div.head: Site of the Old Bridewell.
div.p: The Site of the Old Bridewell.

Sir,—May I ask through you what the authorities intend doing with the ground on which the old Bride- well stood? Several complaints have been made to me as one of the representatives of Howley Ward, by the shopkeepers in larlam-street, about the clouds of dust blowing into their shops in dry weather from this land,doing immense damage to the goods in their shops, and I have seen it for myself. It was my intention—at the request of these shopkeepers—to have raised the question at the Council meeting on Tuesday, but it slipped my memory. lam not quite sure which Com- mittee is .responsible for this work; but it is high time something was done to protect these ratepayers.—Yours etc., COUNCILLOR.

div.head: Park Music.
div.p: Park Music.

notice with very great pleasure that in next Sunday's programme, the chorus 'We never will bow down" (Handel's "Judas Maccabmus") will be played by Messrs. Crosfield's band in the park. Now, this, to my mind, is the class of music that should be presented to us by the bands which appear on the bandstand on Sundays. We have had too much worthless music played in the past, and it is quite time a step was taken towards advancement; moreover we should not allow bazaar music to be played on a Sunday. lam sure I need not specify any: piece, but it will be quite obvious to all musical people what I mean. There is plenty of good music to be had, without bands choosing old, senseless and distressing pieces that we have sometimes presented to us. I should like to suggest that our leading bands give us the "Amen" chorus from "The Messiah," also any popular chorus taken from any well-known oratorio. These, lam sure would be heartily appreciated, and would help to raise the standard of brass bands in this town.—Yours etc.
ONWARD.

div.head: Summer Holidays for poor Children.
div.p: Summer Holidays for poor Children.

Sir,—l should like to call attention through the medium of your columns to the importance of sending poor children into the country for a portion of their summer holiday and to the practical means which may be taken to this end. There is scarcely any need for me to dwell on the advantages the children derive from a change. All who can afford it adopt this plan for their own children, and the children of that section of the community whose earnings are extremely low, who according to Mr. Charles Booth form about 20 per cent. of the population, must suffer more, physically and mentally from a want of change through the very low condition of their vital powers than better fed children. The importance of doing everything that is practicable to improve the health of the children, who are to be Warrington's future citizens will be admitted and few methods are so free from objection as that of sending the children to the sea side to live for a week in a camp where they will be well cared for and be under strict discipline. Feeling strongly the force of the above, I have during the past 10 years by the aid of the School Attendance Officers sent every year about 100 boys who have been selected by the officers as being the most needy to the Summer Camp at Birkdale. The funds have been sub- scribed by a few of our well-knownWarrington citizens. There are many more poor children who ought to have the advantage of this change and I urge the public of Warrington to take this matter up. Hoping that some of your readers will volunteer to join a committee for the purpose of extending this work,—l am, Yours truly, ARTHUR H. LEE.
Brick-street. Warrington, June 12th, 1903.

div.head: Mr. J. Podmore jun., and Trades Unionists.
div.p: Mr. J. Podmore jun., and Trades Unionists.

Sir,—ln reference to remarks made at the Warring- ton Trades Council meeting on Wednesday last week allow me as the late secretary of the liairdressers' Association to take exception to statements made by Mr. J. Podmore jun. on bad Trade Unionists. As one of the two referred to, I emphatically deny that I reso- lutely opposed any advance in the price of shaving, but owing to the situation of ray business I was willing to obtain the 11d, where possible. I am pleased to say that my efforts . have been successful in 150 cases, by supplying each customer with a private pot and brush and fresh water. No doubt, before long this will be general among my customers. I should like to know how this custom compares with the way in which other hairdressers are treating theircustomers. Does this bear out Mr. Podmore's statement when he repliedto a delegate's question at the Council meeting? I should like to ask Mr. Podmore a question. Why did the Hairdressers' Association supply notices of the advance to hairdressers who have never been members of the Association, and thus try to mislead and deceive workingmen ? According to rule 5 of the Hairdressers' Rules, no member is allowed to open on Sun- day and Thursday, afternoon. This rule is not complied with by the hairdressers who have had such notices. I should like to know where the consistency of the Hairdressers' Association rests. I should like to mention that when the advance was first mooted notices were sent out to 48 or 50 hair- dressers and only 24 were present to considerthe matter at the final meeting. When it wasproposed to adopt the advance only 18 -members of the Trade were present and 16 voted in favour of the advance and two against. I think working men will see by the way I conduct my business that I have considered the labourin_g class, and that I am not so bad a trade unionist as I have been painted by Mr. Podmore, after being Secretary of the Association for 17 years.—Yours etc., EDWARD SMITH, (Late Secretary, Warrington Hairdressers' Association).

div.head: Warrington's Roman Remains.
div.p: Warrington's Roman Remains.
Sit,—Very ignorant ideas are still being circulated in regard to the exploration of Warrington's Roman remains, and the valuable and interesting antiquities found in them. _ _ _

The antiquarian societies of the present day, such as the Historic Society of Lancashire and Cheshire,do not print in their transactions anything which is not of real historic importance or not properly verified by scientific and exact data, such as drawings to scale, photographs, &c. The study of archwology has now become a science, for the study of which schools are established in the large centres, such as Liverpool, Manchester, &c., and professional chairs endowed in the leading universities of this country and on the continent. Neither do our up-to-date museums fill their cases with a "routh o' auld kick nackets" as formerly, but all their specimens are aMapted and arranged for the practical teaching of natural and ethnographical science, such as geology, botany, conchology, ,history, &c., and industrial and applied art. In all highly educated communities on the continent, in Germany, France, Switzerland, Italy, Austria, &c., there are Government departments for the custody and preservation of national monuments, and there are national and provincial museums maintained at large cost for the collection and display of specimens. Our own British Museum has now an Anglo-Roman depart- ment for which specimens are purchased out of the annual grants made by Parliament. The trustees of that institution would no doubt be willing to purchase many of the objects found at Wilderspool and Stockton Heath, which are of unique character. If Warrington is to have a museum at all, tho specimens therein ought at any rate to be those of its own locality and those of special interest and value to its own inhabitants—thoseconnected with its own early origin, whereby a reflection of the "Roman glory" is cast upon its past. Allow me to suggest to those who object on the ground of economy to the payment of a small- share—about one-third—of the expense of exploring our Roman remains and acquiring the "finds" for our museum, that these objects have a commercial value and that, on being sold to the trustees of the British Museum or the Smithsonian Institute in America, or to some rich Yankee collector, or even to some other Lancashire or Cheshire municipal museum where the people are more advanced, there would be a profit on the transaction and a few pounds gained for the relief of rates. The sale could be made with the option of repurchase when the objectors have become more prosperous and intelligent under influence of the new Education Act. . .

My own earnest hope and endeavour will be to obtain the support of the great body of the ratepayers in having the exploration of Warrington's Roman remains com- pleted and the relics safely deposited and scientifically arranged in the Musqurn, to illustrate the iron, glass, lead, copper, texile, and other manufactures of our "town of many industries." The present is the cheapest and only time for doing so as the ground will soon be covered with houses and streets.—Yours, &c. THOMASMAY. Lower Walton, 15th June, 1903.

Mr. :John Lewis, manager of the Felinfoel Brewery, near Llanelly, shot himself dead with a revolver on Monday afternoon. Deceased, who was well known throughout South Wales, had been transacting business as usual during the morning. Mrs. Evelyn Thompson, British and Foreign Bible Society's missionary at Shanghai, China, bias been found dead, suspended by a cord attached to the back of a bedroom door at a villa she was visiting on South- borough Common, Tunbridge Wells.

div.p: The Examiner Friday June 19, 1903. FATAL CAB COLLISION. WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT A Warrington Driver's Long Hours. COUNCIL JURY'S EXPRESSION OF OPINION. Longford Depot Nuisance. The monthly meeting of this authority was held at Bewsey Chambers on Wednesday afternoon, Mr. T. Halton presiding :—Messrs. Brooks, Mather, Knowles,Houghton, Dr. Murray, Forshaw, with Dr. Sephton (medical officer), Messrs. J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assist- ant clerk), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), H. H. Burnage (assistant surveyor) and F. lierfoot (inspector of nuisances.)

On Sunday, in the absence of the Pastor, the Rev. John Davies, of Warrington preached morning and evening at the Baptist church, Golborne street. in his evening sermon, the preacher pointed out the lessons which could be learned from the life of the martyr Stephen.

Buckley street Methodist Free Church. The Sunday school anniversary sermons were preached on Sunday last by Mr. R. B. Woods, of Latchford. The services were largely attended. The spacial hymns and anthems sung by the children reflected credit on the conductor, Mr. James Ryder. Miss M. Plinston was the organist. In the afternoon a mission service was presided over by Mr. J. Balt, and an address was given by Mr. Woods. The followin.g solos were much appre- ciated :—" Queen of the Angels," by Miss L. Fairhurst "There is a green hill," by Mr. Percy George; "Children of the city " and " The good shepherd," by Miss A. Bridge; "If with all your heart" and" The children's home," by Mr. A. Greenough. Mr. B. Butcher also contributed a violin solo with pleasing effect. Mr. Albert E. Trow was the accompanist.

A cab collision resulting in the death of William Jesse Richard Jinks, aged 16 years, son of a cab driver residing in Factory-yard, occurred in Chester New-road, Warrington, on Saturday evening. The circumstances were detailed at the inquest which was conducted at the Police Station on Tuesday afternoon by Mr. S.Brig- house, countycoroner. Mr. R. Crompton appeared on behalf of the relatives of the deceased, Mr. A. J. Willett for Mr. Arthur Wilson, cab proprietor, and Mr. E. A. Connor for Mr. Edward Connor, cab proprietor. Richard T. Jinks, deceased's father, described the collision. Witness was on his near side, the wheels of the cab being in the gutter, and there was at that point room for three conveyances to pass. Witness was driving at between five or six miles an hour. When the approaching cab was about 15 or 20 yards away witness shouted to the driver, who was making straight for him. The cab, however, came on and dashed into witness's vehicle the wheels being locked together. Both he and his son were pitched off the box and witness was dazed for a few minutes, and did not know where he was. When he came to himself his boy was lying on the foot- path, and being attended by Dr. Smith. He was after- wards removed to the Infirmary. Witness was perfectly sober. His lad always accompanied him on Saturday nights. When he saw the other cab coming. he had not time to cross over to get out of the way.—By Mr. Crompton: The road was about 40 feet wide.
Mr. Connor: There is no dispute about the road. It is 36 feet wide.

In answer to Mr. Connor, witness said his horse was going at a walking price when the collision occurred. After the smash Murphy said "You are drank, Jinks." Witness was not short sighted. The driver of the other cab, Christopher Murphy, a youth of eighteen in the employ of Mr. E. Connor, was then called. He stated that he went home at six o'clock on Friday night, and commenced work again cleaning harness alone o'clock on Saturday morning. He was on duty till eleven o'clock on Saturday night. The Coroner: I thought my occupation was hard, but—it is hard cheese with you. Witness, in answer to the Coroner, said he got two or three hours' sleep in the harness room. Continuing, he said he started from "The Elms" at Daresbary on Saturday night to drive Dr. Smith and his wife and Mrs Clare and a gentleman to Warrington. He had had nothing to drink. He did not seethe other cab approach- ing until it was within ten yards of him. Witness's horse shied, dashed across the road aunt the cab swerved into Mr. Wilson's vehicle. Witness was not looking straight' ahead, some people on the footpathhaving at- tracted his attention.

The Coroner: Don't you think it is a "cock and bulj" story to tell? Witness: The horse shied three or four times going to Daresbury, and twice on the way back. The Coroner: Were you not asleep? Witness: No, sir.

The Coroner: Twenty-two hours on duty and only two or three hours' Bleep. You would pop off to sleep very quickly before you knew where you were. Witness: I was not asleep. I was half asleep and half awake.

The Coroner: You might as well admit it. I should go to sleep myself after working 22 hours. Most likely I should have stopped the cab to go to sleep. (Laughter). Mr. Connor is to blame for keeping you on duty so long. You cannot work 22 hours without get- ting sleep. It is ridiculous.

In answer to Mr. Connor, witness said he heard Jinks shout" Heigh, up," but witness replied: "I cannot." He worked seventeen hours on Friday. The Coroner said he would not blame the witness for being asleep. He did not know how the lad had kept awake on the box. Questioned by Mr. Connor, the witness said he could go to sleep in the harness room when he was not required to drive. He usually ceased Work at two or three o'clock in the afternoon.
William Dodson, 4, Smith-street, Lower Walton also described the collision.

Dr. Reginald Smith stated that he was in the cab driven by Murphy. After the collision witness saw the lad on the footpath. He was unconscious and bleeding profusely from the mouth and left ear. Witness saw he was suffering from fracture of the skull and had him removed to thelnfirmary, where he died. He had since made a post-mortem examination, and found the cause of death was pressure on the brain, resulting from the fracture.

The Coroner: Did you notice whether the driver was sleepy or not ?—He seemed quite awake at the start of the journey. Witness said he did not notice anything unusual until the collision occurred and there could not have been shying to any great extent. In summing up the Coroner said that everyone who brought anything dangerous on the highway had to exercise care, skill, and diligence. People were under a wrong impression when they spoke of the right and wrong side of a road. It was only a matter of custom. Having worked so long it would be quite easy for Murphy to go'to sleep for a short time and then waken up. They could not blame the lad, although it was very unfortunate that Jinks had lost his son. They must, however, confine themselves to the issue as to whether the lad himself was really to blame or not, and if they considered he was doing the best he could after having been on duty so long he was not to blame The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," the Foreman stating that they were of.the opinion that the lad Murphy had been on duty too long, and' that such long hours should be put a stop to. If the lad hadnot been working so long he would have been able to keep his eyes open, and they did not think he was to blame for the accident. They thought it was a pity that the Factory Act did not apply in this caso.
RE-APPOIN-rmENTS.
The Local Government Board wrote sanctioning the re-appointments of Dr. Sephton as medical officer of health and Mr. F. Kerfoot as inspector of nuisances for the ensuing year.
THE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

Dr. SEMITON reported that during the month there had been 26 births and 33 deaths, 17 of the deaths occur- ring in Winwick Asylum. The death rate was equal to 359 per 1,000 and exclusive of the deaths at the Asylum to 17*3.

div.head: Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel. Sunday School Anniversary.
div.p: Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel. Sunday School Anniversary.

Despite the unfavourable weather on Sunday, success attended the Sunday School anniversary services in connection with Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel. The morning service was held in the chapel, the preacher being the Rev. J. Howell Jones, of Bolton, one of the leading preachers in the Wesleyan denomination. The rev gentleman preached an ' appropriate discourse which was closely followed bythe congregation. In the afternoon an excellent musical service was held in the Parr Hall, and was well attended, especially considering the unfavourable weather. Mr. Councillor James Dodds presided. The school children occupied seats at the rear of the plat- fonn, most of the girls being attired in white, and the ensemble was a pleasing one. The service commenced with the singing af the hymn" Praise ye the Lord" and afterwaids prayer was offered by the Rev. John Gunnell. The scholars then rendered the chorus " The Gladsome Song" with spirit and expression and their singing gener- ally reflected credit upon the conductor,.Mr.D.B. Dunn. Mr. F, Podmore,M.l.U.M presided at the organ with his usual ability. Two solos entitled "Song of good courage" and "0 Divine Redeemer" were sweetly interpreted by Miss Bessie Eckersley,Mr. Podmore accompanying on the piano. A recitation entitled "A Little Pilgrim" was given with taste and feeling by Miss H. Dunn. The children sang the anthem "Give thanks to God" and two choruses entitled" Gifts of Beauty "and "The King's Army," mall of whichthey acquitted themselves admirably. The CHAIRMAN, in referring to the excellent singing of the children, said it was a great credit to Mr. Dunn, the conductor, and all concerned. The preceding chorus was entitled" Gifts of Beauty "and he had now to appeal for gifts of utility—gifts for the good work now being carried on at Sankey Bridges. They were all interested in Christianity, which alone of all the religions had stood for social,religious and political freedom. Christianity stood alone among the religions for real temperance and for purity in social, private and public life. It stood for human and universal brother- hood seeking for the day when man to man the world o'er shall be brothers. Christianity stood against war, selfishness and pharisaism and all that that meant. It had ennobled womanhood as no other religion had done. It had ennobled home life, it had dignified labour, and it had been a blessing to the children. In the work of propagating Christianity, Methodism had done its share and had done its work well. Warrington Methodism had done its share of the work and those connected with Sankey Bridges might be said to be the stalwarts of Methodism. He pleaded with those present to assist the men and women who were working with quiet heroism at Sankey Bridges. He knew the work that was being carried on there and it was deserving of hearty support. The Rev. JOHN GUNNELL delivered an interesting address, in which he referred to the impending bi-cen- tenary of the birth of John Wesley.. Addressing his remarks chiefly to the younger portion of the audience, he asked them to go back in imagination with him to the days of the old stage waggon, and travel with him to the small market town of Epworth, in Lincolnshire. The preacher proceeded to pay an imaginary visit to the rectory there, an old building, all gables, with a thatched roof. Here on the 17th of June 1703,J0hn Wesley was born. A delicate and frail child from birth fears were entertained of his life and shortly after his birth he was christened John Benjamin Wesley. The preacher proceeded to give a graphic description of the fire at the Rectory when it was burnt to the ground. He alluded to the rescue of Wesley from the burning building at a critical moment by some of the neighbours who saw his form at one of the windows. The founder of Methodism, he said, had a marvellous deliveranae, and his mother regarded it as a token that God had a specialwork for him to do. The subsequent career of Wesley was briefly traced, and mention was made of the new light which entered his mind whereinhe saw that simple faith in Jesus Christ was the only means of salvation. He went preaching that gospel and "the little one became a thousand and the small one a strong nation." To-day although only 200 years had passed since the day of Wesley's birth, the Methodist church was the greatest Protestant church in the world. John Wesley had a larger number of followers in the different branches of Methodismithan any other of the great religious teachers or reformers God ever gave to the world. It would be a standing reproach to them as Wesleyans if they allowed the bi-centenary of Wesley's birth to pass unnoticed. The service concluded with the hearty singing of the hymn" Onward Christian Soldiers." At night, there was again a large congregation, when the Rev. J. Howell Jones preached an effective dis- course. Miss Eckersley gave a pleasing interpretation of the solo "I will give you rest." Collections were taken at each service in aid of the Sunday school funds, and realised the handsome sum of £45 4s. nd.

div.head: SHIP CANAL LITIGATION. Warrington Traders and the Minutes of the Judgment. .
div.p: SHIP CANAL LITIGATION. Warrington Traders and the Minutes of the Judgment. .

In the Chancery 'Division, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Byrne, the action brought by Messrs. J. Cros- field and Sons and other Warrington traders against the Manchester Ship Canal' Company in respect of the failure of the Canal Company to dredge the Mersey at Warrington to a sufficient depth was mentioned.• Mr. Bousfield, K.C.. for the plaintiffs, said that the minutes of the judgment declared that upon the true construction of the Act and the agreement the depth of Bft. meant Bft. of water below the low-water level of spring tides from time to time, and did not mean Bft. below any permanent line. The defendants objected to the words from time to time," as they were not in the Act oragreement, but he contended they ought to be left in.

After hearing Mr. Fletcher Moulton, His Lordship decided that the words must stand, leaving it to the Court of Appeal to set him right, if wrong. Mr. Bousfield said the minutes further declared that plaintiffs were entitled to recover from the defendants all tolls and dues paid by them since August 16, 1899, "under protest," He objected to the words "under pro- test." _ _
Mr. Moulton argued that these words shnuld be re- tained. . _ _

..... lathe result his Lordship inserted the words " under protest or duress." Mr. Moulton pointed out that the minutes further provided that the plaintiffs should recover damages for all injury caused to them by any breach on the part of the defendants" since January 1900. Ho objected to the word "till," which might include relief not intended by the court. His Lordship retained the word, Which meant all injury for which the plaintiffs could recover damages.

div.head: P.S.A. MOVEMENT. Annual Meeting of the Wycliffe Society.
div.p: THE P.S.A. MOVEMENT. Annual Meeting of the Wycliffe Society.
On Sunday,the annual meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society was held. In the absence of the President, the chair was occupied by Mr. R. Atkinson.
LF,TiER FROM THE PRESIDENT.

Prayer having been offered, the secretary read a letter from the Rev. John Yonge, who is staying at Buxton. Mr. Yonge stated that he was very sorry to be away for the first time from theannual meeting. He hoped the re- sult of the meeting would be to encourage all to give themselves a new to:earnest and united endeavour to make

the P. S. A. of greater use than events history hitherto had been happy and prosperous and it ()Illy needed that every man should his hearty share towards increasing the membership and awakening enthusiasm. Enthusiasm was essential to success. The younger men should buckle on the armour and become valiant for Christ. There were crowds of men who might be reached with personal and united effort. Surely it was worth while trying ! Were there not 20 or 30 of the brethren who would band together to go Sunday by Sunday to enlist recruits? The P.S.A. should become aggressive and missionary. Other Sun- day afternoon meetings were already making aggressive endeavours to gather in new members. Why should the Wycliffe P.S.A. be idle when others were active? Very earnestly did he hope that something would be attemp- ted.

div.head: ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: ANNUAL REPORT.

Mr. B. FARRAR (hon. secretary) presented the tenth annual report and stated that they were not to be dis- couraged because their numbers had not gone up. It ought to be a stimulus to greater effort and determined effort. So long asj there were so many workingmen who went to no place of worship on the Lord's Day it was their duty to try and bring them inside their meet- ing places to hear the Gospel, that their thoughts should be guided aright their inclinations directed towards God, their homes made brighter, their wives and children helped to a higher and nobler life. A high spiritual tone had been maintained at the meetings, the Chairmen and speakers keeping to the moral and spiritual side of the subjects referred to. Mr. Payton had been responsible for the musical portion of the services and had served them well. The year closed with an enrolled membership of 567 or 7 less than the previous year, with Jui averageattendance of 370. During the year 706 prizes were distributed making a total distribution of 9,246 prizes since the commence- ment of the Society. The usual merit cards had been given to those making regular attendance. The sick club was still doing a good work and had a membership of about 70. The Savings Club had 110 depositors and there would be a sum of about £l7O or £lBO distributed for the Walking Day holidays. During the present year the members enrolled numbered 466 which was an increase upon last year. Reference was made by the secretary to the losses by death and to the new arrange- ments which had been made for visiting those who were sick or in trouble. In conclusion, Mr. Farrar urged the members to take a deeper interest in all that apper- tained to the prosperity of the Society.
T-HF, BALANCE SHEET.

_ Mr. R. Atkinson (hon. treasurer) submitted the annual balance sheet. The year commenced Iv ith balance in hand of 3d. and closed with a debit of .21 13s. 7d. The income was £l2O 12s. 11d, and the ex- penditure £122 6s. 6d. Mr. R. MILLS presented a report on absentee visita- tion and Mr. JOSEPH OWEN submitted a report and statement of accounts in connection with the Benevolent fund.
The reports were adopted. ELECTION OF OFFICERS AND COMM ITTEE.

The following officers were re-elected: President, Rev. John Yonge; general secretary, .Mr. B. Farrar; assistant secretary, Mr. A. Dowries; treasurer, Mr. R. Atkinson; registration secretary, Mr. A. Cotterill ; benevolent fund secretary and treasurer, Mr. Jsseph Owen; absentee secretary, Mr. R. Mills: markers, Messrs. W. and H. Farrar: steward, Messrs. J. Lankford and T. Wood; committee, Messrs. W. H. Payton, W. Beswick, J. Bailey, W. W. Crosskill, A. Healey, 0. Wallington. G. Smilev, J. Sinicock, J. Garner, 0. Colley, C. Cotton, D. Ried, J. Dobbins, P. Palmer, A. Ashton, J. Gresty, J. West, J. Hallam, J. Starkey, W. E. Appleton, John Lester, J. E. Massey, J. Riley, J. Burton.

div.p: TfIE PROPOSED IMPROVEMENTS.

Messrs. lit:Wwne-i;;u1-6.-:on-ii,1-0-W,- solicitors, wrote en- closing copy of a communic2tion from the Town Clerk stating that the work and experiments ordered by the Town Council at Longford dept were being proceeded with as quickly as possible.
